**About New York Festival of Song**  
 Now in its 38th season,**[New York Festival of Song (NYFOS)](https://u7061146.ct.sendgrid.net/ls/click?upn=u001.VKhd6YigfG0GnZnvTYQEBifsBkU1H2oSSJVrSJZbYPg-3DiDX8_kh-2BkvUQ70fULTiohBTD3D3ykhWbzoPdlET1TB5P-2F0vsbjhHGaA7kq0xQzTVlMd3bh9Zzwcy4N5VHp6hYhYQiK4u7ppRdXjOo89iFyEAP4wkSOlpL1QDEIU0lEpsXohpGpMFseWA1O82-2BVzGoA9JlPq-2Fa41siZ4xFv6KbxD1Qen6c91hG4LqFcZrqGB6SRi-2FU8nrRZRz4k-2FJbD9P0-2BgykHj69jzdWpfobcYF80l-2FiaXwXMuR-2FLJHhIgQHN695O7GntnRtxNFJOASlKJ6vMW4eGOjgHMa-2BEk0giRAlRpWkfpK7pykbWzV2UwM06kagPT6m9vDnAlqMN4nFX12LTyknzg-3D-3D)**is dedicated to creating intimate song concerts of great beauty and originality. Weaving music, poetry, history, and humor into evenings of compelling theater, NYFOS fosters community among artists and audiences. Each program entertains and educates in equal measure.  
  
 Founded by pianists Michael Barrett and Steven Blier in 1988, NYFOS continues to produce its series of thematic song programs, drawing together rarely-heard songs of all kinds, overriding traditional distinctions between musical genres, exploring the character and language of other cultures, and the personal voices of song composers and lyricists.  
  
 Since its founding, NYFOS has particularly celebrated American song. Among the many highlights is the double bill of one-act comic operas,_Bastianello and Lucrezia_, by John Musto and William Bolcom, both with libretti by Mark Campbell, commissioned and premiered by NYFOS in 2008 and recorded on Bridge Records. In addition to _Bastianello and Lucrezia_ and the 2008 Bridge Records release of _Spanish Love Songs_ with Joseph Kaiser and the late Lorraine Hunt Lieberson, NYFOS has produced five recordings on the Koch label, including a Grammy Award-winning disc of Bernstein’s _Arias and Barcarolles_, and the Grammy-nominated recording of Ned Rorem’s _Evidence of Things Not Seen_(also a NYFOS commission) on New World Records. In 2014,_Canción Amorosa_, a CD of Spanish song—Basque, Catalan, Castilian, and Sephardic—was released on the GPR label, with soprano Corinne Winters accompanied by Steven Blier.  
  
 In January of 2022, NYFOS Records issued its first album,_From Rags to Riches_, with Stephanie Blythe and William Burden. In January of 2025, they released their sixth album,_Schubert/Beatles_, with Theo Hoffman, Julia Bullock, Kunal Lahiri, and Mr. Blier. The new CD joins NYFOS Records’s burgeoning discography, alongside _A Picnic Cantata_(2022), the first stereo recording of a hidden gem by Paul Bowles and James Schuyler;_Black & Blue_(2023), the debut solo album of British-American tenor Joshua Blue collaborating with Steven Blier;_Mi País: Songs of Argentina_(2023) featuring bass-baritone Federico De Michelis and pianist and Steven Blier; and _NYFOS Records: The Singles, Vol. 1_(2024), a wide-ranging compilation drawn from over 20 years of archival material, including tracks featuring Michael Spyres, Justin Austin, and Bernarda Fink. NYFOS Records has reached rapidly growing audiences in over 100 countries, with well over 2.5 million streams to date.  
  
 In November 2010, NYFOS debuted NYFOS Next, a mini-series for new songs, hosted by guest composers in intimate venues, including OPERA America's National Opera Center, National Sawdust, the DiMenna Center for Classical Music, the Ann Goodman Recital Hall at Kaufman Music Center, and now the Rubin Museum in Chelsea.  
  
 NYFOS is passionate about nurturing the artistry and careers of young singers, and has developed training residencies around the country, including with The Juilliard School’s Ellen and James S. Marcus Institute for Vocal Arts (now in its 17th year); Caramoor Center for Music and the Arts (its 17th year in March 2025); San Francisco Opera Center (over 20 years as of February 2018); Glimmerglass Opera (2008–2010); and its newest project, NYFOS@North Fork in Orient, NY.  
  
 NYFOS’s concert series, touring programs, radio broadcasts, recordings, and educational activities continue to spark new interest in the creative possibilities of the song program, and have inspired the creation of thematic vocal series around the world.  
  
**About Steven Blier**  
**Steven Blier**is the Artistic Director of the New York Festival of Song (NYFOS), which he co-founded in 1988 with Michael Barrett. Since the Festival’s inception, he has programmed, performed, translated and annotated more than 150 vocal recitals with repertoire spanning the entire range of American song, art song from Schubert to Szymanowski, and popular song from early vaudeville to Lennon-McCartney. NYFOS has also made in-depth explorations of music from Spain, Latin America, Scandinavia and Russia._New York Magazine_ gave NYFOS its award for Best Classical Programming, while _Opera News_ proclaimed Blier “the coolest dude in town” and in December 2014,_Musical America_ included him as one of 30 top industry professionals in their feature article, “Profiles in Courage.”  
  
 Mr. Blier enjoys an eminent career as an accompanist and vocal coach. His recital partners have included Michael Spyres, Renée Fleming, Cecilia Bartoli, Samuel Ramey, Lorraine Hunt Lieberson, Susan Graham, Jessye Norman, and José van Dam, in venues ranging from Carnegie Hall to La Scala. He is also on the faculty of The Juilliard School and has been active in encouraging young recitalists at summer programs, including the Wolf Trap Opera Company, the Steans Institute at Ravinia, Santa Fe Opera, and the San Francisco Opera Center. Many of his former students, including Julia Bullock, Stephanie Blythe, Sasha Cooke, Paul Appleby, Dina Kuznetsova, Corinne Winters, and Kate Lindsey, have gone on to be valued recital colleagues and sought-after stars on the opera and concert stage. In keeping the traditions of American music alive, he has brought back to the stage many of the rarely heard songs of George Gershwin, Harold Arlen, Kurt Weill and Cole Porter. He has also played ragtime, blues and stride piano evenings with John Musto. A champion of American art song, he has premiered works of John Corigliano, Paul Moravec, Ned Rorem, William Bolcom, Mark Adamo, John Musto, Richard Danielpour, Tobias Picker, Robert Beaser, Lowell Liebermann, Harold Meltzer, and Lee Hoiby, many of which were commissioned by NYFOS.  
  
 Mr. Blier’s extensive discography includes the premiere recording of Leonard Bernstein’s _Arias and Barcarolles_(Koch International), which won a Grammy Award;_Spanish Love Songs_(Bridge Records), recorded live at the Caramoor International Music Festival with Lorraine Hunt Lieberson, Joseph Kaiser, and Michael Barrett; the world premiere recording of _Bastianello_(John Musto) and _Lucrezia_(William Bolcom), a double bill of one-act comic operas set to librettos by Mark Campbell; and _Quiet Please_, an album of jazz standards with vocalist Darius de Haas, and _Canción amorosa_, a CD of Spanish songs with soprano Corinne Winters. His latest releases for NYFOS Records include _Black & Blue_(2023), with British-American tenor Joshua Blue;_Mi País: Songs of Argentina_(2023) with bass-baritone Federico De Michelis; and _NYFOS Records: The Singles, Vol. 1_(2024), a compilation of guest artists performing together with Steven Blier, spanning over 20 years of memorable moments and voices.

A native New Yorker, he received a Bachelor’s Degree with Honors in English Literature at Yale University, where he studied piano with Alexander Farkas. He completed his musical studies in New York with Martin Isepp and Paul Jacobs. Mr. Blier is a Yamaha Artist.

# New York Festival of Song Announces 2025–26 Programming

 Jun 26, 2025 

!Image 9

_![Image 10: NY Festival of Song](https://assets.simpleviewinc.com/simpleview/image/upload/c\_fill,h\_200,q\_75,w\_300/v1/clients/newyorkstate/NY\_Festival\_of\_Song\_0f3c55a7-5302-41e3-91d7-3b3d37075e67.jpg)Four-Concert Mainstage Series Co-Presented with Kaufman Music Center at Merkin Hall Begins November 20_

_Season Additionally Includes NYFOS Next Festival at The Theater at 150 W 17 and NYFOS Residency at The Juilliard School_

**New York, N.Y. (June 26, 2025)**—New York Festival of Song (NYFOS), led by Artistic Director Steven Blier, today announces its 2025–26 season of performances, including four Mainstage Series programs at Merkin Hall, co-presented with Kaufman Music Center. The season also includes the _​​NYFOS Next_ Festival at The Theater at 150 W 17 and NYFOS’s annual residency at The Juilliard School.

“Our 38th season reunites me with some beloved colleagues—a trio of powerhouse baritones, a pair of charismatic sopranos, and of course that force of nature known as Bénédicte Jourdois, who will partner with me at many of the Mainstage programs,” Steven Blier said. “The season we've created is a series of duet concerts that place American song in consecutive dialogue with music from France, Germany, and South America. (There are, blessedly, no travel bans on song.) To expand our horizon, we’ll also offer our Caramoor program—a dazzling international collection of ocean voyages and river trips, filled with adventure and sensuality. I’m very eager to share the music with you!”

NYFOS kicks off its Mainstage season at**Merkin Hall at Kaufman Music Center**on**Thursday, November 20, 2025 at 8:00 p.m.**with _**South America, North America: A Love Story**_. Created for baritone**Joseph Parrish**, a Baltimore native, and Bolivian soprano**Shelén Hughes**(partners on- and off-stage) and accompanied by Steven Blier, this program explores the music of North and South America through the milongas, tangos, blues, and art songs that span the two continents.

The Mainstage season continues on**Thursday, February 12, 2026 at 8:00 p.m.**with _**Fugitives**_, featuring baritone**Justin Austin**and a guest co-star to be announced later in the season; Steven Blier and**Bénédicte Jourdois**will be at the piano. A revival of an acclaimed program last heard in 2008, the playlist includes songs from the concert stage, the movies, Broadway, and Berlin’s cabarets, tracing the varied fates of the composers who faced destruction during Hitler’s rise to power—some to begin new lives and brilliant careers abroad, others to meet with darker ends. The concert features works by Kurt Weill, Franz Schreker, Alexander Zemlinsky, Friedrich Hollaender, Kurt Tucholsky, Erich Korngold, Hanns Eisler, and many others.

On**March 11, 2026 at 8:00 p.m.**NYFOS offers _**To the Sea**_, highlighting the brilliant young talents of Caramoor’s 2026 Schwab Vocal Rising Stars program as they take a musical dive into the world’s rivers and oceans, with songs by Elgar (including his magnificent _Sea Pictures_), Fauré, Guastavino, Rachmaninoff, Brahms, Pauline Viardot, and many others. During a weeklong residency at the Caramoor Center, pianists and curators Bénédicte Jourdois and Steven Blier mentor these musicians, resulting in a concert of special power. Former participants have included Julia Bullock, Paul Appleby, Joélle Harvey, and John Brancy; this year’s group is the latest in that distinguished 17-year tradition.

NYFOS concludes its Mainstage season at Merkin Hall with _**Poulenc / Sondheim**_ on**Tuesday, April 7, 2026 at 8:00 p.m.**Poulenc’s sensuality is the perfect foil for Sondheim’s lightning wordplay in this program showcasing two contrasting masters of irony, musical wit, urban sophistication, and psychological acumen. The concert stars soprano**Christine Price**and baritone**Theo Hoffman**, with pianists and curators Bénédicte Jourdois and Steven Blier.

NYFOS continues to release albums and singles throughout the season on its in-house label,**NYFOS Records**. Their latest CD,**_Schubert/Beatles_**(January 2025), based on an adventurous 2016 NYFOS program, features a star-studded cast including baritone**Theo Hoffman**, soprano**Julia Bullock**, tenor**Andrew Owens**, and pianists**Kunal Lahiri**and Steven Blier. This new recording follows in the wake of**_The Singles, Vol. 1_**(2024), a collection of treasured performances spanning over 20 years of NYFOS’s history; and _**Mi país: Songs of Argentina**_(2023) reveling in the spellbinding delicacy of Argentina’s art songs and tangos, with bass-baritone**Federico De Michelis**and Steven Blier. Both albums received rave reviews and thousands of streams online. **About New York Festival of Song**  
 Now in its 38th season,**[New York Festival of Song (NYFOS)](https://u7061146.ct.sendgrid.net/ls/click?upn=u001.VKhd6YigfG0GnZnvTYQEBifsBkU1H2oSSJVrSJZbYPg-3DiDX8_kh-2BkvUQ70fULTiohBTD3D3ykhWbzoPdlET1TB5P-2F0vsbjhHGaA7kq0xQzTVlMd3bh9Zzwcy4N5VHp6hYhYQiK4u7ppRdXjOo89iFyEAP4wkSOlpL1QDEIU0lEpsXohpGpMFseWA1O82-2BVzGoA9JlPq-2Fa41siZ4xFv6KbxD1Qen6c91hG4LqFcZrqGB6SRi-2FU8nrRZRz4k-2FJbD9P0-2BgykHj69jzdWpfobcYF80l-2FiaXwXMuR-2FLJHhIgQHN695O7GntnRtxNFJOASlKJ6vMW4eGOjgHMa-2BEk0giRAlRpWkfpK7pykbWzV2UwM06kagPT6m9vDnAlqMN4nFX12LTyknzg-3D-3D)**is dedicated to creating intimate song concerts of great beauty and originality. Weaving music, poetry, history, and humor into evenings of compelling theater, NYFOS fosters community among artists and audiences. Each program entertains and educates in equal measure.  
  
 Founded by pianists Michael Barrett and Steven Blier in 1988, NYFOS continues to produce its series of thematic song programs, drawing together rarely-heard songs of all kinds, overriding traditional distinctions between musical genres, exploring the character and language of other cultures, and the personal voices of song composers and lyricists.  
  
 Since its founding, NYFOS has particularly celebrated American song. Among the many highlights is the double bill of one-act comic operas,_Bastianello and Lucrezia_, by John Musto and William Bolcom, both with libretti by Mark Campbell, commissioned and premiered by NYFOS in 2008 and recorded on Bridge Records. In addition to _Bastianello and Lucrezia_ and the 2008 Bridge Records release of _Spanish Love Songs_ with Joseph Kaiser and the late Lorraine Hunt Lieberson, NYFOS has produced five recordings on the Koch label, including a Grammy Award-winning disc of Bernstein’s _Arias and Barcarolles_, and the Grammy-nominated recording of Ned Rorem’s _Evidence of Things Not Seen_(also a NYFOS commission) on New World Records. In 2014,_Canción Amorosa_, a CD of Spanish song—Basque, Catalan, Castilian, and Sephardic—was released on the GPR label, with soprano Corinne Winters accompanied by Steven Blier.  
  
 In January of 2022, NYFOS Records issued its first album,_From Rags to Riches_, with Stephanie Blythe and William Burden. In January of 2025, they released their sixth album,_Schubert/Beatles_, with Theo Hoffman, Julia Bullock, Kunal Lahiri, and Mr. Blier. The new CD joins NYFOS Records’s burgeoning discography, alongside _A Picnic Cantata_(2022), the first stereo recording of a hidden gem by Paul Bowles and James Schuyler;_Black & Blue_(2023), the debut solo album of British-American tenor Joshua Blue collaborating with Steven Blier;_Mi País: Songs of Argentina_(2023) featuring bass-baritone Federico De Michelis and pianist and Steven Blier; and _NYFOS Records: The Singles, Vol. 1_(2024), a wide-ranging compilation drawn from over 20 years of archival material, including tracks featuring Michael Spyres, Justin Austin, and Bernarda Fink. NYFOS Records has reached rapidly growing audiences in over 100 countries, with well over 2.5 million streams to date.  
  
 In November 2010, NYFOS debuted NYFOS Next, a mini-series for new songs, hosted by guest composers in intimate venues, including OPERA America's National Opera Center, National Sawdust, the DiMenna Center for Classical Music, the Ann Goodman Recital Hall at Kaufman Music Center, and now the Rubin Museum in Chelsea.  
  
 NYFOS is passionate about nurturing the artistry and careers of young singers, and has developed training residencies around the country, including with The Juilliard School’s Ellen and James S. Marcus Institute for Vocal Arts (now in its 17th year); Caramoor Center for Music and the Arts (its 17th year in March 2025); San Francisco Opera Center (over 20 years as of February 2018); Glimmerglass Opera (2008–2010); and its newest project, NYFOS@North Fork in Orient, NY.  
  
 NYFOS’s concert series, touring programs, radio broadcasts, recordings, and educational activities continue to spark new interest in the creative possibilities of the song program, and have inspired the creation of thematic vocal series around the world.  
  
**About Steven Blier**  
**Steven Blier**is the Artistic Director of the New York Festival of Song (NYFOS), which he co-founded in 1988 with Michael Barrett. Since the Festival’s inception, he has programmed, performed, translated and annotated more than 150 vocal recitals with repertoire spanning the entire range of American song, art song from Schubert to Szymanowski, and popular song from early vaudeville to Lennon-McCartney. NYFOS has also made in-depth explorations of music from Spain, Latin America, Scandinavia and Russia._New York Magazine_ gave NYFOS its award for Best Classical Programming, while _Opera News_ proclaimed Blier “the coolest dude in town” and in December 2014,_Musical America_ included him as one of 30 top industry professionals in their feature article, “Profiles in Courage.”  
  
 Mr. Blier enjoys an eminent career as an accompanist and vocal coach. His recital partners have included Michael Spyres, Renée Fleming, Cecilia Bartoli, Samuel Ramey, Lorraine Hunt Lieberson, Susan Graham, Jessye Norman, and José van Dam, in venues ranging from Carnegie Hall to La Scala. He is also on the faculty of The Juilliard School and has been active in encouraging young recitalists at summer programs, including the Wolf Trap Opera Company, the Steans Institute at Ravinia, Santa Fe Opera, and the San Francisco Opera Center. Many of his former students, including Julia Bullock, Stephanie Blythe, Sasha Cooke, Paul Appleby, Dina Kuznetsova, Corinne Winters, and Kate Lindsey, have gone on to be valued recital colleagues and sought-after stars on the opera and concert stage. In keeping the traditions of American music alive, he has brought back to the stage many of the rarely heard songs of George Gershwin, Harold Arlen, Kurt Weill and Cole Porter. He has also played ragtime, blues and stride piano evenings with John Musto. A champion of American art song, he has premiered works of John Corigliano, Paul Moravec, Ned Rorem, William Bolcom, Mark Adamo, John Musto, Richard Danielpour, Tobias Picker, Robert Beaser, Lowell Liebermann, Harold Meltzer, and Lee Hoiby, many of which were commissioned by NYFOS.  
  
 Mr. Blier’s extensive discography includes the premiere recording of Leonard Bernstein’s _Arias and Barcarolles_(Koch International), which won a Grammy Award;_Spanish Love Songs_(Bridge Records), recorded live at the Caramoor International Music Festival with Lorraine Hunt Lieberson, Joseph Kaiser, and Michael Barrett; the world premiere recording of _Bastianello_(John Musto) and _Lucrezia_(William Bolcom), a double bill of one-act comic operas set to librettos by Mark Campbell; and _Quiet Please_, an album of jazz standards with vocalist Darius de Haas, and _Canción amorosa_, a CD of Spanish songs with soprano Corinne Winters. His latest releases for NYFOS Records include _Black & Blue_(2023), with British-American tenor Joshua Blue;_Mi País: Songs of Argentina_(2023) with bass-baritone Federico De Michelis; and _NYFOS Records: The Singles, Vol. 1_(2024), a compilation of guest artists performing together with Steven Blier, spanning over 20 years of memorable moments and voices.

A native New Yorker, he received a Bachelor’s Degree with Honors in English Literature at Yale University, where he studied piano with Alexander Farkas. He completed his musical studies in New York with Martin Isepp and Paul Jacobs. Mr. Blier is a Yamaha Artist.

## Introduction

I decided to write this essay on music after a recent conversation with my sister Jeanne regarding the [“Mozart effect”](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5586918/pdf/mpp-0023-0403.pdf) after she read an article about it. The Mozart effect, simply stated, posits that listening to the music of [Mozart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wolfgang_Amadeus_Mozart), specifically [Mozart’s sonata in D for two pianos](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tT9gT5bqi6Y) is therapeutically beneficial. Specifically, there are “neurobiological effects of music suggest(ing) that auditory stimulation evokes emotions linked to heightened arousal and result in temporarily enhanced performance in many cognitive domains.”

I shared with her my recent discovery of a 100 minute music therapy suite, called Omnisonix, by the Cellist [Michael Fitzpatrick](https://www.michaelfitzpatrick.com/music-1), the [award winning musician](https://www.talentforhumanity.org/about-us/creative-celebration-circle/michael-fitzpatrick) who has performed around the world, including for Popes, Kings, Presidents and the Dalai Lama. He is not to be confused with another [Michael Sean “Fitz” Fitzpatrick, whose music as leader of the band Fitz and the Tantrums](https://www.forbes.com/sites/jimryan1/2020/03/24/michael-fitzpatrick-and-noelle-scaggs-of-fitz-and-the-tantrums-on-maintaining-optimism-all-the-feels/) I really like.

Jeanne and I had a great discussion, and I again realized the importance of music in my own life, as well as its importance in the culture at large. This is a big topic. I could have attempted an essay like I [did with the topic of history](https://medium.com/@jylterps/what-is-history-and-why-should-we-care-a-perspective-6d1b4daf51ec), and titled this “What Is Music?,” but that would have been a book or several books, not an essay. Besides, I am not a [musicologis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musicology)t, just someone who likes to listen to music, and occasionally create it, like billions of other human beings.

I am now seventy years old, and only started writing essays and publishing them in the last two years. In several of them, I continue to reference songs and song lyrics. As an art form and as an emotional release and expression, music, specifically songs with singing of lyrics, are an important part of my life so why not write an essay about music and its importance in my life and in the larger culture? In fact, I often quote specific song lyrics that capture emotional release as expressed in song by [Joni Mitchell](https://jonimitchell.com/) — “[laughing and crying, you know it’s the same release.”](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=H2Uo5oe9-NM)

A good place for a broad overview could be the [Wikipedia entry for music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music) and [music history](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_music). They provide good perspectives to help one grasp the significance of music in all our lives throughout the history of humanity. If one is religious, you could also check out the [many references to music in the Bible](https://bible.knowing-jesus.com/topics/Music). So, I have decided to write an autobiographical essay on music in my life after first addressing some cultural and metaphysical and evolutionary aspects of the importance of music in human culture and possibly beyond. To borrow a turn of phrase from a friend and a popular concept in general, this will be a part of “my life in song.”

Music is the Universal Language

## Music basics

The detection, processing and appreciation of music first begins with the sense of hearing. Music can be enhanced by activating other senses such as sight, touch and movement, and can be enhanced by other chemical bodily adjustments either from natural processes or by ingesting mood and perception-altering drugs, or by combining movement in dance and theater. Music consists of created sounds in the absence of silence.

Having said that, the [deaf can and do experience music](https://www.hearinglikeme.com/how-the-deaf-experience-music/). “For many people with hearing loss, music is experienced differently.” They can “access the full spectrum of sound through the beat,” or in the case of the [“feel the music program”](https://www.mahlerchamber.com/learning/education-and-outreach/feel-the-music-programme) run by the Mahler Chamber Orchestra, hearing impaired children may experience music by touching “different parts of the instruments — literally feeling the sound waves the music produces — and learn how to watch the movements of the musicians to understand the rhythm and emotion of the music.”

Music [is a sound](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sound) that has an [acoustical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acoustics) structure which include types of [tones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musical_tone), [harmony](https://hellomusictheory.com/learn/harmony/) and [rhythm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm). Music is a beautiful (or ugly) noise that is not silence. German Philosopher [Thomas Metzinger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Metzinger) in his recently published book [The Elephant and the Blind](https://direct.mit.edu/books/oa-monograph/5725/The-Elephant-and-the-BlindThe-Experience-of-Pure), which is the result of the many (>1000) interviews with committed meditators from over 50 countries, as part of the [Minimal Phenomenal Experience Project](https://mpe-project.info/the-mpe-project/) (MPE) had this to say about silence:

“The American composer, artist, and music theorist [John Cage (1912–1992](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Cage)) wrote about a sudden philosophical insight that he had in the late 1940s during an experiment in the anechoic chamber at Harvard University. He described it like this: “[S]ilence is not [**_acoustic_**](https://dictionary.cambridge.org/dictionary/english/acoustic). It is a change of mind, a turning round.” Philosophers and artists have ignored the phenomenology of silence for too long, and finally giving it serious attention raises many interesting questions. Can there be a kind of music that brings the silence between two sounds into the foreground?

What exactly is common to all kinds of music that makes silence, the space between two notes, audible? More generally, are there forms of art that can “stage” MPE, to “orchestrate” the silence of pure awareness itself? Could there be an aesthetic of acoustic emptiness? And on the mental level — in the mind of the meditator — are there ways to actively imagine a sound and then let it go? Are there what today’s computational modelers might call mental “action policies”:17 paths into nonaction that will reliably create the experience of silence?”

One of my favorite musical artists, improvisational jazz pianist [Keith Jarrett](https://www.keith-jarrett.de/en), actually produced an album titled [“Silence,](https://www.allmusic.com/album/silence-mw0000083094)“ with a [beautiful song of the same name](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ph7s7uowKQY). Nearly all of Jarrett’s music is improvised, even [when playing standards](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NHGx_6w-lmU), but his [1975 Koln concert](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=skkiVoI7sBk) is a masterpiece of beautiful improvisation — he plays it as he is writing it or creating it, a simultaneous process.

While it is true that most music composition has silent spaces between the musical notes, this essay will be about the totality of music our ears can hear and our bodies can feel, including the silence in between the notes.

If we were to simplify music as an acoustic sound that is produced such that it may be heard by the creator and other listeners, it can be broken down into component parts. These include:

- **Creation and Production** — manipulating [vocal cords](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vocal_cords) during exhaling, aka [singing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singing), striking something to create resonance, like the strings of a [guitar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guitar), [violin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Violin), [cello](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cello), or those struck by the keys from a keyboard as with a [piano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano); blowing air through something to create a specific sound. This is done primarily through singing and playing a musical instrument, whether a wind instrument, such as a[trumpet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trumpet), [saxophone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saxophone), or [flute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flute); a stringed instrument or some percussive instrument, such as a [drum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drum) or other percussion instrument, or even clapping of one’s hands. With the conversion of [analog music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comparison_of_analog_and_digital_recording) into [digital form](https://aimm.edu/blog/equipment-beginning-music-producer-needs), there are now a wide variety of digital devices that can also produce sounds and music. I will later reference Rick Beato’s discussion of what this has done to music appreciation.

- **Composition** — the process of combining all elements of sound into a song also known as songwriting.

- **Performance** — the ability to create music and present it to others, the listeners.

- **Appreciation and criticism**. Listeners of music who like what they hear or don’t like what they are hearing or who like to explain the cultural, political or artistic significance of what everyone is hearing. Listeners get together in different cultural contexts to compare their different types of appreciation, positive and negative.

When listening today (7/11/2024) to [WETA classical radio](https://weta.org/fm), the DJ referenced a [“Hurdy Gurdy” instrument](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurdy-gurdy). I thought, she can not be referring to the 1968 hit song by [Donovan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donovan), [Hurdy Gurdy man](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CHxfOZH8cew), the only other time I have heard that term. She was not, she was referencing the 10th century instrument. My musical education was not formal, but informal, obviously.

## Music as foundational in evolution, and the “cultural universal language”

In the 19th century, the poet Henry Wadsworth Longfellow wrote, “Music is the universal language of mankind.” A [recently completed study conducted at Harvard](https://news.harvard.edu/gazette/story/2019/11/new-harvard-study-establishes-music-is-universal/) confirmed this claim. The late musicologist [Linda Shaver-Gleason](https://www.amsmusicology.org/news/503457/Linda-Shaver-Gleason-1983-2020.htm)[took issue with this claim](https://notanothermusichistorycliche.blogspot.com/2018/01/is-music-universal-language.html) of Longfellow, but did so before the Harvard study was published. The study in part was seeking to establish whether the claim was true, and to provide a scientifically based study as a citation for others making this claim.

The study sought to find out “which musical qualities overlap across disparate societies?” The study team collected music from around the world that contained “nearly 5,000 descriptions of songs from 60 human societies.” The study participants “Mehr, Singh, and Glowacki call this database [The Natural History of Song](https://www.themusiclab.org/nhs). One observation of the study was that music appeared in every society in the world that they observed. Across these societies music [is associated with behaviors](https://news.harvard.edu/gazette/story/2018/01/music-may-transcend-cultural-boundaries-to-become-universally-human/) “such as infant care, healing, dance, and love” and “among many others, like mourning, warfare, processions, and ritual. They discovered that songs that share behavioral functions tend to have similar musical features.”

Another fascinating theory, this one by only one person and less scientifically rigorous, is the theory proposed by Jóse Díez Faixat, who is an architect, non-violent conscientious objector, ecologist, and rural community member.

Faixat’s [music theory of evolution](https://www.integralworld.net/faixat1.html) is a “harmonious solution” to enable a better understanding of the [nature of evolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evolution), which he asserts has a “spiral rhythm.” Faizat’s theory “proposed hypothesis is very simple: just as in any musical instrument successive second harmonics (1/3 of the vibrating unit) progressively generate new sounds; these same second harmonics generate all the major evolutionary novelties in universal dynamics as a whole.”

“We were saying that the supposed solidity of matter, upon which the world was supposedly raised, has faded away before the gaze of New Science into pure forms and relationships within an abstract, insubstantial fabric. Thus, the ancient dispute between several Greeks schools arises once again in our time. While for [Ionic philosophers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ionian_school_(philosophy)) the most important issue consisted in discovering the corporeal substance of the world, for the [Platonic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Platonism) and [Pythagorean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pythagoreanism) schools the key was to be found in patterns and orders. The science of today essentially moves along this second line of thought.

The most fundamental statement of the Pythagoreans was that numbers constitute the unmovable principle of the world, the very essence of reality. When they discovered that the proportions among musical harmonics could be expressed in a simple and exact form, they considered that the cosmos itself was a harmonious system of numerical reasoning: all reality could be expressed by means of relationships among numbers. According to the Pythagorean’s, the inherent numerical order of sounds was directly related with the very organization of the universe. For them, music was therefore nothing other than the expression of the inner relationships of the cosmos. They even affirmed that all material manifestation was the result of the concert of universal vibrations.”

## My Musical Beginnings

I am a baby boomer, [“born in the 50s” (1954),](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=23JntUfxjoM) with three siblings. Our parents were the WWII generation, and we grew up listening to the few records they had and the radio stations they played around the house. [Cool Water](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cool_Water_(song)) was a song I used to sing as a three-year-old, with my Aunts mimicking my repeating as a young boy, “record player, record player” over and over again. It was written in 1936 and first recorded by the [Sons of the Pioneers](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rr8pd6egb5s) on March 27, 1941.

That was on my birthday, 13 years before I was born but during a hugely important time in my parents’ lives, their early 20s and the beginning of the seminal event of the 20th century, WWII. It is possible the ’45 record I was playing was the 1955 version of the song by [Frankie Laine and the Mellomen.](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9K1Vpm2OFCY) As I listen to these two versions today, I can not for sure remember which version I was playing all the time as a young boy, but think it might have been the Pioneers version, which my parents may have first heard when they began dating as teenagers in the late 1930s. In researching this, I think I like the [Marty Robbins 1959 version](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=j-3UiPy-iOM) best though.

While the [invention of Radio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Invention_of_radio) was in the late 19th century, it rose to prominence in the mid-20th. President Franklin Roosevelt used the medium effectively communicating to Americans with his [“fireside chats”](https://www.whitehousehistory.org/the-fireside-chats-roosevelts-radio-talks) during the Great Depression and during the [“golden age” of radio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Age_of_Radio) (1920s-1950s), prior to [Television launching and displacing it](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_television) as the preferred medium. My wife and I [saw a play in 2019, “On Air”](https://dctheaterarts.org/2019/05/14/on-air-creative-cauldron/) which features the rise of radio programming which included the playing of music and songs.

In his 1977 song, [Radio, Radio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radio_Radio), [Elvis Costello](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elvis_Costello) sang “Radio is a Sound Salvation, Radio is Cleaning up the Nation.” Elvis’s song effectively sang about a medium that really enabled the blossoming and spread of music and music appreciation in the west and around the world. Prior to music on the airwaves, one had to purchase a record and have the money to own a record player, or go listen to a music creator perform their music live. Radio enabled artists to reach a much wider audience and increase the popularity of all kinds of music. Eventually, songs heard on the radio determined which records and CDs loyal listeners and fans would buy.

With the spread of television in the 1950s and 1960s, audiences added a visual depiction of the artists they had only previously heard and imagined when they came across the radio. When Elvis Presley appeared on TV on the [Milton Berle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milton_Berle) show, then [Ed Sullivan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ed_Sullivan_Show), [he created quite a stir within the culture with his shaking hips](https://americansongwriter.com/remember-when-elvis-was-censored-from-the-waist-down-on-the-ed-sullivan-show/), causing producers to not show him below the waist. It is hard to imagine that time now with a [song and video like Cardi B’s WAP, from 2021](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hsm4poTWjMs). Uh, times have changed.

I grew up listening to [AM station WLEE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WLEE_(1480_AM)) in Richmond VA, and this is where my interest in music really began with the hit songs of the 1960s. By the time I reached High School, a syndicated [DJ “Cosmic Cowboy” Shane Gibson](https://www.insideradio.com/people_moves/shane-brother-shane-gibson/article_3d43aa1c-7146-11eb-ae60-3b42c9536060.html) was reaching and influencing teenagers in Richmond and around the country along with shows such as [Casey Kasem’s American Top 40](https://www.wusf.org/arts-culture/2020-07-03/50-years-ago-casey-kasem-began-counting-down-the-hits-on-american-top-40).

## Music lessons — performing music vs just listening to it

While my parents played music around the house, other than my mother singing along to some of her favorite show tunes or songs by Italian singers like Frank Sinatra, Jerry Vale, Dean Martin and others, or my father playing the harmonica, they did not practice music or play it. They did, however, insist that all of their children learn to play an instrument. My two older sisters took piano lessons and my younger brother learned to play the trumpet in public elementary school.

My sisters and I went to private Catholic school for much of our K-7 education so there was no musical instruction in school. So, when it came time for me to learn an instrument I selected the drums. I had private lessons for about a year or two and had a [practice drum pad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Practice_pad) and eventually a [Slingerland Ace White snare](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-o1oD6bBpNo) at home to practice outside on the back porch. I never owned a full drum kit as a child. In the 1990s, I housed the childhood drumkit of my wife’s nephew Todd for 10 years and that was the first time I ever played on a full drum kit. Todd and I would jam together, trading places on drums and electric guitar. That was technically my 2nd band after my junior high school concert band edition.

With my drum lessons, I learned the basics, proper hand position holding sticks, [the roll](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JQ9VlK-tUyQ), [flams](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5ujmfxvr0bQ),[paradiddles](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=h0OoVP6VgBE), and counting basic beats. While it is true that there was not too much singing in Catholic churches then, I did sing some in the Mass as part of my alter boy duties and before my voice changed with puberty, I could actually hold a tune and sing on key.

Jeanne later taught herself to play guitar and so did my trumpeter brother John. As an adult, John played with other guitarists around Richmond in adult living residences and has also performed for our family and at talent shows in his apartment complex. Jeanne’s oldest son Jesse was a [music major at VCU, majoring in voice,](https://arts.vcu.edu/academics/departments/music/) but he also taught himself guitar and some piano and has maintained a collection of instruments around his house for his three children. Jesse also performed [Italian arias](https://imslp.org/wiki/24_Italian_Songs_and_Arias_of_the_17th_and_18th_Centuries_(Various)) at family reunions, and funerals. [Franz Schubert’s](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franz_Schubert)[Ave Maria](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XpYGgtrMTYs) is a staple at Italian occasions and that was one Jesse performed on several occasions, including the 90th birthday of our late Aunt Rena, my mother’s older sister. My other sister Joy’s grandchildren are now taking piano lessons and according to Uma-grandma, they are pretty good. I have yet to validate this claim!

When I enrolled in public Junior High School Brookland in 1966, for grades 7–9, I learned there was a school concert band and elective class, so I enrolled in it. I played in the percussion section but unlike most of my classmates, I had no prior musical instruction in school and did not know how to read music and had to learn it on the fly during class. During my three years in that band, I played the snare drum, the bass drum, [clave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clave_(rhythm)), [triangle (idiophone),](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triangle_(musical_instrument))[maracas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maraca),[glockenspiel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glockenspiel), and the [Timpani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timpani) (two kettle drums tuned to Eb and Bb mostly).

The Timpani and other bass instruments had music notated in bass clef, vs normal [treble or G clef](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clef). So not only did I have to learn treble clef and learn about whole, half, eighth and sixteenth notes and musical timings on the fly, I had to translate to read it in bass clef whose notes were one step below treble clef on the sheet music. Fortunately for me, we only had two Timpani drums and only two notes — one high and one low! For the other percussion, there were no musical notes, just timing for when to strike the percussive instrument.

My favorite story was when we did a Christmas Concert for the school community and parents and [played the song Sleighride](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xTMc-WAjL-I). The end of that song has a whip crack and I had to invent the sound to the satisfaction of our band teacher, Mr. Louis LeGrand, who also happened to be a 2nd Clarinet performer in the [Richmond Symphony Orchestra.](https://www.richmondsymphony.com/) We did not have the [wooden clapper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clapper_(musical_instrument)) used in the Navy band performance linked above.

There was a plywood wall riser behind the percussion section on the stage and I used a 12 inch wooden ruler and held one end and pulled back on the other end and timed it to create the snap sound we needed, pleasing Mr. LeGrand and the band. Mr. LeGrand was somewhat of a perfectionist and had high expectations for his students.

By the 9th grade, he did something with our band during summer school he had never done, he entered us in a County wide competition where each band was graded on their performance by a panel of judges. Mr. LeGrand was quite disappointed when we did not win and only received a grade of “C” for our performance. Mr. LeGrand also did another thing with us he had never done; we performed a classical number (I can’t remember which one) featuring a solo for Clarinet and he performed it with us, playing the clarinet solo.

There were at least two of my classmates from that time in the Brookland band that went on to play music in high school and later for most of their adult lives. Two years younger than me was a Sax player named [Les Owen](https://www.linkedin.com/in/les-owen-51b8aa13/). Les went on to enlist in the US Army and played Baritone sax and vocals in [The Jazz Ambassadors](https://www.armyfieldband.com/about/ensembles/jazz-ambassadors), The US Army field band, and the Alto sax in the [US Army Ceremonial Band, otherwise known as “Pershing’s Own.](https://www.usarmyband.com/ensembles/the-u-s-army-ceremonial-band)” Les later formed his own documentary film company called [treehouse dreams films](https://www.treehousedreamsfilms.com/), producing some great work there, including a profile of the [valedictorian of my 1972 high school graduating class, Spence Ford](https://www.treehousedreamsfilms.com/defining-passion/v/defining-passion-the-dancer-4740).

Another guy in my class and concert band was 1st trumpeter [Al Dieste](https://cheguayaba.wixsite.com/website). As an adult, when Al was not umpiring MLB games in AZ spring training, Al went on to perform during his adult life in California, Florida and Georgia under various band names and under his own name. Beyond playing trumpet, Al sang and performed keyboards in several bands. Here is Al [performing on youtube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HLfQj4LoUQ0) and a writeup about him with his previous band [Tropical Madness.](https://www.gigsalad.com/al_dieste_and_tropical_madness_modesto)

When it came time for me to enter High School at [Hermitage High School](https://hermitage.henricoschools.us/) in 1969, I was forced to decide. I could either play in the high school band or play football, but not both. The band director had a requirement that to be in the band one must attend all practices and participate in all marching band activities, including halftime at football games. The football coach and athletic director, old school [Chester E. Fritz](https://www.legacy.com/us/obituaries/timesdispatch/name/chester-fritz-obituary?id=5362534), (Hermitage High School would later rename their stadium after him) would not allow one to consider doing both, [something that I have read about over the years with many kids doing this at different schools since that time](https://turnto10.com/sports/perfect-10/somerset-berkley-regional-high-school-starting-football-player-marching-band-drums-bristol-county-massachusetts).

I chose football, which essentially ended my formal musical education. I no longer played the drums until I was an adult in my 40s. The Hermitage band went on to establish quite a tradition. Here is a [2010 Richmond Magazine profile](https://richmondmagazine.com/news/hes-with-the-band-03-26-2010/) of the band after my time there in the early 1970s. A non-musician football teammate who also lived in my neighborhood, [Jimmy Jinkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Jinkins), went on to a successful career as an animator and cartoonist and created the successful 1990s [cartoon “Doug”,](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doug_(TV_series)) which was loosely based on his time growing up in Henrico County VA and attending Hermitage and playing for coach Fritz.

## Music and Physical Performance — Priming, Inspiration and Incitement.

The leadership and personal development coach and author [Jamie Wheal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamie_Wheal), who is also co-founder of the [Flow Genome Project](https://www.flowgenomeproject.com/), breaks down [Performance Priming Practice](https://hiitscience.com/enhancing-performance-prime/) into four elements for achieving peak performance in any endeavor. These are:

- Breathing,

- Moving,

- Fueling (what one eats and drinks),

- **Listening to Music**.

Wheal notes “music primes your mind and heart for high performance. Depending on many factors, including the beats per minute (BPM) in a song, you can up-regulate or down-regulate your system to overcome the challenge ahead. [Michael Phelps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Phelps) shared that he listened to [Eminem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eminem) and [EDM music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronic_dance_music) in his Performance Priming Practice before races.” ESPN discussed the [top 10 “hype hits”](https://www.espn.com/espn/feature/story/_/id/29435103/top-10-sports-songs-get-stadium-arena-hyped) used to prime performers and inspire and incite fans alike and this Eminem song was # 6 on that list.

If anyone watches sports regularly, whether in person or on TV, you observe both the athlete’s using music prior to performance and the host teams using music to inspire and incite the crowd and athletes in unison. Certainly most athletes believe that [music makes them a better performer](https://www.pbs.org/newshour/science/can-music-make-you-a-better-athlete).

#7 on the ESPN list was [Jack White’s](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_White)[Seven Nation Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seven_Nation_Army) used globally by everyone — seen here at [Baltimore Orioles MLB baseball playoff game](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tt4cR9szMS8). This song is all about the riff and repetitive motif. It uses this [musical motif](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motif_(music)) or [riff,](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riff) just like Beethoven’s [opening to his 5th symphony](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=n3EiRynr1Us) or the opening chords to the Jethro Tull [song Aqualung](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N4zPu3ISCGs).

Interestingly, this ubiquitous song at sporting events in the USA first started to be used in European soccer matches, even though White is American and released the song first in the US, then it migrated to American football games, then basketball, then baseball. It is now a [“universal sports anthem.”](https://americansongwriter.com/how-the-white-stripes-seven-nation-army-became-the-universal-sports-chant/)

Music has also always been associated with sporting events with traditional songs played during the events — the National Anthem played at the beginning of the contest and in baseball with [Take Me Out to the Ballgame](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=eItTJehqMIQ) played during the seventh inning stretch and with the Baltimore Orioles also including [John Denver’s Thank God I’m a Country Boy, including changing the last refrain from “riddle” to “rid-OOOOOOO.”](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9r-lVbUk7GA)

Baseball has also inspired songwriters to write about that sport, including the late Chicago musician [Steve Goodman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Goodman) with his ode to Cubs, [A Dying Cubs Fan’s Last Request](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ewnTNlNBXGw). Sadly, Steve died long before the Cubs finally won the World Series again in 2017. Former Creedence Clearwater Revival leader [John Fogarty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Fogerty) wrote his song [Centerfield,](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Xq3hEMUeBGQ)an anthem often played at the beginning of the baseball season.

Sports fandom is or can be a tribal phenomenon, as say [politics are now](https://www.newyorker.com/news/daily-comment/a-new-report-offers-insights-into-tribalism-in-the-age-of-trump). If a fan supports their team, they associate themselves with that team and they feel part of that team’s tribe. If other teams from the other tribe have music associated with it, tribal fans like me can develop negative connotations with the music of that team, even if an objective viewing of the song means under normal circumstances, one would like the song. I have been tribal in my fandom, and [made it onto the B1G network as a result](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6WbwbU-2ASk).

My teams that I root for are the teams of my alma mater, the University of Maryland, and professional teams are the Baltimore Orioles and Ravens. I have had these rooting interests for over fifty years. Before that, it was my high school Alma Mater, Hermitage High School.

Some examples of songs associated with other teams that create a negative reaction from me whenever I hear them include:

- [We Are Family](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hB4eGNYMDKQ) ([Sister Sledge](https://sistersledge.com/))– associated with Baltimore Orioles losing to the Pittsburgh Pirates in the 1979 World Series, many Orioles fans I have spoken with have a similar visceral reaction when hearing this song.

- [New York, New York](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HzBzTsDuzeg) ([Frank Sinatra](https://www.sinatra.com/)) — associated with the New York Yankees, played after they win a game. Sadly, I really like Frank Sinatra, but not this one, I can not disassociate this context from hearing it.

- [Sweet Caroline](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4F_RCWVoL4s), ([Neil Diamond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Diamond)) — played at [Boston Red Sox](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KxAk1aL-BNo) and [Penn State football](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NDPdV_HwVwI) games. My wife is a big Neil Diamond fan, I like him too, but this song is not in any playlist for me. I switch it off when it comes on. I have a sickness in my stomach when heard in these contexts, and it’s such a great song with a wonderful chorus, what a shame.

## Music Appreciation through history

Another way to appreciate music is to visit historical sites associated with the creation and playing of music. Since I retired in 2011, my wife and I have been able to visit several such sites. These include:

- Memphis, TN [Stax museum](https://staxmuseum.org/), where the great [“Stax Sound”](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stax_Records) was produced.

- Memphis TN — [Sun Recording Studio Museum](https://www.sunstudio.com/), where [Elvis Presley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elvis_Presley), [Carl Perkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Perkins) and [Jerry Lee Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerry_Lee_Lewis) recorded in the 1950s.

- Nashville, TN — [Grand Ol Opry](https://www.opry.com/), [Ryman auditorium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ryman_Auditorium), [Country Music Hall of Fame and Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_Music_Hall_of_Fame_and_Museum).

- Austin TX, [“Live Music Capital of the World”,](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_of_Austin,_Texas) multiple music clubs and [Austin City Limits](https://www.austincitylimits.com/).

- Tupelo, MS — Elvis Presley’s [birthplace, original home and museum](https://elvispresleybirthplace.com/visit/).

- [Mississippi Blues Trail](https://msbluestrail.org/) along Highway 61.

Perhaps our favorite stop was [Muscle Shoals, AL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muscle_Shoals,_Alabama), site of the Muscle Shoals Sound Studio.

In 2022, during a trip cycling and driving along the [Natchez Trace Parkway](https://www.nps.gov/natr/index.htm), a “trip through 10,000 years of history,” we visited the [Muscle Shoals Recording Sound studio](https://muscleshoalssoundstudio.org/), whose documentary one can watch [on streaming platforms](https://www.watchnow.com/movie/muscle-shoals/41445?t_source=64&gad_source=2). Located in northwestern Alabama, one can also visit the nearby [memorial to Te-lah-nay](https://www.natcheztracetravel.com/natchez-trace-alabama/florence-tennessee-river/456-wichahpi-stone-wall.html), the Native American teenage girl, part of the [Yuchi tribe](https://tennesseeencyclopedia.net/entries/yuchi-indians/), and learn the story of her removal in 1839 by the US government as part of the [trail of tears forced mass migration and relocation of native Americans](https://www.nps.gov/liri/learn/historyculture/the-trail-of-tears.htm) and her return trip five years later.

In the documentary, [this story is told briefly by her Great Great Grandson, Tom Hendrix](https://www.onlyinyourstate.com/alabama/longest-unmortared-wall-al/), who spent 32 years building the memorial to honor her story. When we visited, we met a man from Louisiana returning for the fourth time. He told a story as relayed to him by Tom (now deceased) when a car pulled up and a Native American Chief and his traveling partner arrived. According to the driver of the car, the Chief had not spoken in two weeks. He got out, walked around the memorial, then walked up to Tom and said, “I will now speak.” He said he had been on a quest to find the appropriate memorial honoring a great American woman and he found it there.

It is indeed a very spiritual place and perhaps not a coincidence that in the area where Te-la-nay heard the Tennessee River singing, and returned because when she was removed to Oklahoma, the rivers there did not sing. As a teenager, she traveled alone for five years to return home. There is this place in a remote part of northwest Alabama where recording studios appeared where some of the greatest American music ever made was recorded, where a Native American girl heard the river sing.

## Singer-Songwriter, Americana Music

The year 2013 was an interesting year in music for me and for my wife.

Over the entire time we have known each other, we have attended many live music performances at many venues in the USA. However, neither of us has been a big music festival attender, too many people, too large of music venues. When traveling in the panhandle of Florida, we heard on the radio of a songwriter’s music festival happening Martin Luther King holiday weekend — the [30A Songwriters Festival](https://www.30asongwritersfestival.com/). We were too late to attend that year, but traveled to the [Cultural Arts Alliance of Walton County](https://www.culturalartsalliance.com/), the sponsors of the festival, and signed up to volunteer and did so for six years until 2019, and plan to return in 2025.

There are many things we like about the festival: many venues, small in size, and great songwriters. Many of the performers are Nashville songwriters, who typically sell their songs to better known performers but at this festival they perform themselves. Most of the music performed would be classified as [Americana Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Americana_music). We discovered many artists we had never heard of before. Among these were: [Wil Kimbrough](https://www.willkimbrough.com/), [Mary Gauthier](https://www.marygauthier.com/), [Jason Isbell](https://www.jasonisbell.com/), [Charlie Mars](https://charliemars.com/), [Steve Poltz](https://www.savingcountrymusic.com/from-a-jewel-video-to-a-folk-hero-rediscovering-steve-poltz/), [Chris Stills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Stills), [Liz Longley](https://www.lizlongley.com/) (who I actually learned of through the Intro to songwriting course) and many, many others. Here is a video performance of the late [Lari White](https://lariwhite.com/), performing [at the festival in January of 2016](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zF9JmmS9bJA). She also had a cameo performance in the movie [Cast Away](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cast_Away).

Recently, another similar festival started much closer to home for us, the [Annapolis Songwriters Festival](https://www.annapolissongwritersfestival.com/), held in September in Annapolis, MD. This one is based on a very popular festival in Key West FL, which I have never attended, the [Key West Songwriters Festival](https://www.keywestsongwritersfestival.com/), usually held in May. The connection between these two is that the owner of a popular Annapolis music hall, the [Rams Head On Stage](https://www.ramsheadonstage.com/), splits his time between Annapolis and Key West[. He bought the rights to the Key West Festival and puts it on in Annapolis.](https://bizmonthly.com/news/business/anne-arundel-county/2022/06/rams-head-bmi-launching-annapolis-songwriters-festival%EF%BF%BC%EF%BF%BC%EF%BF%BC/)

## Introduction to Songwriting, Berklee College of Music, Coursera

In the fall of 2013, I completed an Introduction to Songwriting course from the [Berklee College of Music](https://www.berklee.edu/) that was offered via the educational streaming platform, [Coursera](https://www.coursera.org/). The course was taught by [Pat Pattison](https://www.patpattison.com/). The course syllabus said all were welcome, no prior experience was required. My own view is that a basic understanding of music gained from prior experience was extremely helpful. While I had been a fan of great songwriting my entire life, I never tried writing any songs so I thought I would give it a shot. Among Pat’s previous students were [John Mayer](https://johnmayer.com/) and Liz Longley. It was a great course, that as constructed then, is no longer available on Coursera.

From what I have read and heard before; every songwriter has their own unique method for writing songs. [The muse comes](https://www.masterclass.com/articles/writing-tips-for-getting-inspired) to them in a variety of ways. As someone who sold consulting services, I liked the idea of a “method” or approach. I suppose this was true because I am not really a creative artist, but even those can and have benefited from a process, a way to help with their muse in finding their voice to express it in a song. The songs in question here are [“singer-songwriter”](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singer-songwriter) type songs, namely songs with lyrics and music.

Pat Pattison is a teacher from the Berklee College of Music, and he is one of the great teachers — someone extremely knowledgeable and passionate about his material, who was also an interesting and entertaining presenter. He also offers his services independently. He has written several books on songwriting.

The songwriting taught in the class was for popular songs — namely those with lyrics and melody and harmony that you can sing along with and tap your feet to. In other words, it was not a course on how to write an instrumental jazz composition in 13/8 time or the score to a Classical Music composition.

Pat’s method starts with the idea and emotion, and asking the question- who is speaking in the song and who are they speaking to? Methods are taught to capture the essence of the song then the method first focuses on lyrics — the process of poetry, rhyming and emphasis within a measure. Most of the focus was placed here, as no musical experience is required, but some proficiency with the English language was required and desirable.

Song structure and its uses were explained — verse, chorus and bridge, along with the concept of [“prosody”,](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prosody_(music)) or how all the elements of a song work together to support the central message of the song (i.e. melody, rhythm, lyrics, rhyming structure). Pat then taught about melody and a little about rhythm. Since this was an Introduction course, the latter parts were only covered to the degree necessary to enable the student to write and record a song for a grade. I took the course pass/fail.

Lots of interesting technology was used in the course. I learned about [Soundcloud](https://soundcloud.com/discover), which was new at the time. It was used then and now extensively to upload and download songs and song fragments digitally recorded with a software program like [Audacity](https://www.audacityteam.org/), one of many available on the market. It is free, I used it with my crude ear plugs and microphone in my laptop computer, and my acoustic guitar. This platform is now regularly used by many musicians — from the student or experimenter, to the committed artists, to professionals. So, the student will need software and a computer that will allow for recording yourself and editing to enable overlaying (if desired) music with lyrics.

As mentioned previously, we saw Liz Longley at the 30A Songwriters festival but I first heard her sing in this course as Pat used Liz as part of his teaching as she was a former Berklee College graduate.

She was used by Pat and another Nashville songwriter, who was a former instructor at Berklee, to resurrect a song [“Pieces”](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KTo5GgTRc9s) that they had partially written but had not finished. Liz sang for them as they changed the song. Pat showed how the song evolved, how they changed it with changes in pace, timing and emphasis, using the methods he was teaching, turning it into the final version featured here. When we saw Liz the following year at 30A, we introduced ourselves and discussed the course with her. Her career has moved forward with several albums and tours since then. When we saw her recently in Washington DC at the [now closed City Winery](https://www.songkick.com/concerts/40507989-liz-longley-at-city-winery-dc), she was returning to touring after becoming a mother for the first time.

Lastly, as a study of evolution and “[Big History](https://bighistory.org/),” I appreciated Pat’s brief lecture on the history of song titled “Why We Sing,” which was based on the book [Why Do People Sing, Music in Human Evolution](https://www.amazon.com/People-Sing-Music-Human-Evolution-ebook/dp/B00RQQ4U6G/ref=sr_1_1?crid=293TFV1OY19VU&dib=eyJ2IjoiMSJ9.MqV9fWZetMa9yzkPu39Y1kEz29iRq_FSoL3MpOvadbg.tLedb83JkzaK1xPbH15X8eU1aDlUf4tFZZnvbsdRFLs&dib_tag=se&keywords=why+do+people+sing+in+human+evolution+joseph+jordania&qid=1720814202&s=books&sprefix=why+do+people+sing+in+human+evolution+joseph+jordania%2Cstripbooks%2C79&sr=1-1), by [ethnomusicologist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethnomusicology) and [evolutionary musicologist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evolutionary_musicology)[Joseph Jordania](http://www.josephjordania.org/), 2011, 2015.

“The general conclusion is that choral singing is a very ancient phenomenon which is gradually disappearing all over the World. The third chapter is dedicated to the search for the evolutionary function of music in human and hominid prehistory. After a detailed review of the existing models of the music origins from the ancient times until today, a new model of the origin of music is then suggested.

The new hypothesis is based on the model of Audio-Visual Intimidating Display to defend hominids from ground predators, to assist them in aggressive scavenging and also in confrontations with competing hominid groups. The ability of synchronous group rhythmic singing to transfer humans into the altered state of consciousness, a neurologically induced specific state, a Battle Trance, where humans do not feel pain and fear, is discussed.”

In other words, our ancient ancestors learned to sing to one another before speaking to each other. We learned to sing before speaking languages.

One of the funny aspects of listening to songs and song lyrics is the phenomenon of a [Mondegreen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mondegreen), which is mis-hearing a lyric sung by the performer — e.g. CCR’s “[There’s a Bad Moon on the Rise](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zUQiUFZ5RDw)” becomes “There’s a bathroom on the right.” It is useful to find an official lyric sheet before singing along with a song!

## Teaching Music and Music Appreciation

Everyone who learns to create or appreciate music has a teacher who influenced them. Even if one is self-taught, just listening to others create music has an impact and influences how one may create their own music. I have a former work colleague and former adult slow-pitch softball teammate named [Greg Lefelar](https://www.linkedin.com/in/greg-lefelar-643b45/) (Greg played baseball shortstop in College at Wake Forest University) who also plays electric guitar. Other than being a great IT professional, leader, good husband, father, son and all-around nice guy, Greg also taught himself how to play guitar.

He noodled around for years while working long hours and raising his family. Later in life, he began to really work at getting better and when he had to sponsor a sales event for his company, and hire entertainment, he decided to recruit people from his company to have a band that would do a short set of songs. This launched his efforts at getting better at guitar and it eventually led to his forming his band, playing in his church band, and recruiting some of them to form the band which has played around the DC-Baltimore area. They are now called [Off Color](https://www.gigsalad.com/off_color_germantown). I have seen them several times and they are quite good and fun to be around.

Greg and I used to exchange guitar stories and have a running discussion about the best guitarists, he saying [Keith Richards](https://www.keithrichards.com/) is terrible, me saying Richards is one of the great innovators, song writers and band leaders. As in his work career, Greg is a great technician on the guitar and appreciates guitar players that are as well. I think he believes Keith’s [Open, 5-string G tuning](https://www.cbc.ca/music/read/keith-richards-explains-the-5-string-guitar-5-strings-3-notes-2-hands-and-1-asshole-1.5086421) was a cheap trick and a crutch covering his weak guitar playing skills. As this [Society of Rock article notes](https://societyofrock.com/the-reason-keith-richards-play-a-5-string-guitar/), Keith’s “approach to guitar playing is not centered on flashy or lightning-fast techniques. Instead, it revolves around crafting great riffs, infectious grooves, and timeless songwriting.” Those are all characteristics I really appreciate, never learning to play lead guitar myself.

In one of those conversations recently, Greg mentioned to me a YouTube channel he regularly watches, [Rick Beato](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rick_Beato), and his [Everything Music](https://www.youtube.com/@RickBeato) channels, currently with over 4.3M subscribers. I am now a regular watcher and subscriber of that channel.

Rick is a long-time musician, multi-instrumentalist, producer, music appreciator, and now music educator. In one of [his earlier videos](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=t3Cb1qwCUvI), he showed how his young son has [perfect or absolute pitch](https://news.uchicago.edu/explainer/what-is-perfect-pitch). When Rick’s wife was pregnant, he always had a music boom box near her playing a wide range of music. At a very young age, his son had perfect pitch.

Rick’s two channels feature in depth analysis of music, including “[What Makes This Song Great?”,](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLW0NGgv1qnfzb1klL6Vw9B0aiM7ryfXV_) interviews with musicians, and segments teaching song writing and playing of instruments. It is one of the better musical channels on YouTube. The music is mostly popular rock and roll and jazz, but Rick also covers classical music. A great example of this is his [What Makes Bach Great?](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kcvUHdhROrk)In this short video, The [Bach Effect, What the Greats Hear That You Don’t,](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UNgrH8u-IIc&t=423s) Rick extracts from his many interviews what modern musicians had to say about Bach’s effect and influence on their work. Rick reveals that it was his experience as a young boy playing [Bach’s Brandenberg Concerto’s which](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NCPM8DEsvmc) inspired him to become a musician.

Rick also offers his analysis of how music creation has changed with technology, and not necessarily for the better. Here, he discusses [“The Real Reason Why Music is Getting Worse.”](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1bZ0OSEViyo) He is of course referring to today’s popular music with the many “content creators” and what is happening with the explosion of digital, IT tools, including [Artificial Intelligence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artificial_intelligence). The result is that young people now value music less because:

- Creating music is now too easy

- This process is now homogenizing music

- There is a tremendous quantity of music, but much less quality.

I must mention another artist that as far as I know, has yet to be featured on Beato’s channel — [Ian Anderson and Jethro Tull](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Anderson). I have been a fan of their music since the early 1970s. Tull also performed a Bach number, [Bouree,](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N2RNe2jwHE0) from Tull’s 2nd [album in 1969, Stand Up](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stand_Up_(Jethro_Tull_album)). Anderson was also interviewed in a documentary about Beethoven called “[World Without Beethoven](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ls5XWu4PhSs)?,” [one of many that have been made about Beethoven](https://www.documentarytube.com/best-of/the-12-best-documentaries-about-beethoven/). Ah yes, motifs and [riffs, you have to love em](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JrxZ33l-DTc)!

## Conclusion

Music is universal, it is a big part of what makes us human and part of the larger Kosmos. We could all aspire to appreciate it, create it, and teach it like Rick Beato has. Music’s therapeutic and performance enhancing effects could make us and the world around us a little bit better. As Michael Fitzpatrick has said, “music is the only thing that can change the world.” It is a key aspect of what we define as good, true, and most importantly, beautiful. We have a lifetime to do so. However, as Ian Anderson wrote and sang, “[Life’s a Long Song](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CDqw4wi2PwU), but the tune ends to soon for us all.”

Perhaps what the world needs now is for the [Hurdy Gurdy man](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CHxfOZH8cew) to show up in a big way:

“Histories of ages past

Unenlightened shadows cast

Down through all eternity

The crying of humanity

’Tis then when the Hurdy Gurdy Man

Comes singing songs of love

Then when the Hurdy Gurdy Man

Comes singing songs of love.”

I suppose that with all my recent moving and downsizing, getting rid of my golf clubs, softball equipment, my 850-LP album collection and turntable (I’ve kept 100+ CDs) and other items I no longer use, I still persist in holding onto my guitar and few percussion pieces, so that if I choose to, I may return to them to create some human-created music.

Hurdy Gurdy, Hurdy Gurdy, Hurdy Gurdy. Hurdy Gurdy, Hurdy Gurdy, Hurdy Gurdy.

## Introduction

I decided to write this essay on music after a recent conversation with my sister Jeanne regarding the [“Mozart effect”](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5586918/pdf/mpp-0023-0403.pdf) after she read an article about it. The Mozart effect, simply stated, posits that listening to the music of [Mozart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wolfgang_Amadeus_Mozart), specifically [Mozart’s sonata in D for two pianos](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tT9gT5bqi6Y) is therapeutically beneficial. Specifically, there are “neurobiological effects of music suggest(ing) that auditory stimulation evokes emotions linked to heightened arousal and result in temporarily enhanced performance in many cognitive domains.”

I shared with her my recent discovery of a 100 minute music therapy suite, called Omnisonix, by the Cellist [Michael Fitzpatrick](https://www.michaelfitzpatrick.com/music-1), the [award winning musician](https://www.talentforhumanity.org/about-us/creative-celebration-circle/michael-fitzpatrick) who has performed around the world, including for Popes, Kings, Presidents and the Dalai Lama. He is not to be confused with another [Michael Sean “Fitz” Fitzpatrick, whose music as leader of the band Fitz and the Tantrums](https://www.forbes.com/sites/jimryan1/2020/03/24/michael-fitzpatrick-and-noelle-scaggs-of-fitz-and-the-tantrums-on-maintaining-optimism-all-the-feels/) I really like.

Jeanne and I had a great discussion, and I again realized the importance of music in my own life, as well as its importance in the culture at large. This is a big topic. I could have attempted an essay like I [did with the topic of history](https://medium.com/@jylterps/what-is-history-and-why-should-we-care-a-perspective-6d1b4daf51ec), and titled this “What Is Music?,” but that would have been a book or several books, not an essay. Besides, I am not a [musicologis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musicology)t, just someone who likes to listen to music, and occasionally create it, like billions of other human beings.

I am now seventy years old, and only started writing essays and publishing them in the last two years. In several of them, I continue to reference songs and song lyrics. As an art form and as an emotional release and expression, music, specifically songs with singing of lyrics, are an important part of my life so why not write an essay about music and its importance in my life and in the larger culture? In fact, I often quote specific song lyrics that capture emotional release as expressed in song by [Joni Mitchell](https://jonimitchell.com/) — “[laughing and crying, you know it’s the same release.”](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=H2Uo5oe9-NM)

A good place for a broad overview could be the [Wikipedia entry for music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music) and [music history](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_music). They provide good perspectives to help one grasp the significance of music in all our lives throughout the history of humanity. If one is religious, you could also check out the [many references to music in the Bible](https://bible.knowing-jesus.com/topics/Music). So, I have decided to write an autobiographical essay on music in my life after first addressing some cultural and metaphysical and evolutionary aspects of the importance of music in human culture and possibly beyond. To borrow a turn of phrase from a friend and a popular concept in general, this will be a part of “my life in song.”
