### Seasons 1–10 (1997–2007)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_View&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Seasons 1–10 (1997–2007)")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ad/Barbara_Walters.jpg/250px-Barbara_Walters.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Barbara_Walters.jpg)

Broadcast journalist [Barbara Walters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbara_Walters "Barbara Walters") created the series and co-hosted it from 1997 to 2014.

_The View_ premiered with four co-hosts: Meredith Vieira as moderator, Star Jones, Debbie Matenopoulos, and Barbara Walters.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-nytimes-18) Joy Behar, who filled in as the fourth co-host when Walters was unavailable, soon became a full-time co-host.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-19) The five women were the first group that auditioned for the panel, with Behar describing them as having immediately clicked.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-20) Following Matenopoulos's firing in December 1998, broadcast journalist [Lisa Ling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisa_Ling "Lisa Ling") was brought on as a new co-host in 1999.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-21)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-Slate-22) Ling departed the show in December 2002 to host the series _[National Geographic Explorer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National\_Geographic\_Explorer "National Geographic Explorer")_.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-Slate-22) Former _[Survivor: The Australian Outback](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Survivor:\_The\_Australian\_Outback "Survivor: The Australian Outback")_ castaway [Elisabeth Hasselbeck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elisabeth_Hasselbeck "Elisabeth Hasselbeck") replaced Ling beginning November 24, 2003, after Hasselbeck, television personality [Rachel Campos-Duffy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Campos-Duffy "Rachel Campos-Duffy"), and actress [Erin Hershey Presley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erin_Hershey_Presley "Erin Hershey Presley") each received a week-long on-air tryout.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-24)

In 2006, Vieira left the show to become co-anchor of the [NBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBC "NBC") morning program _[Today](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Today\_(American\_TV\_program) "Today (American TV program)")_;[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-25) her final episode aired on June 9.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-26) That same month, Jones also left the show. Her departure, originally scheduled for July, was brought forward by Walters, publicly feeling "betrayed" by Jones for unexpectedly announcing her departure two days ahead of schedule.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-27) She also said ABC executives had decided not to renew Jones's contract due to diminished approval for Jones through their market research.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-28) Jones later claimed the decision to leave was not hers and that producers informed her that they would not be renewing her contract in April.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-29)

During the [33rd Daytime Emmy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/33rd_Daytime_Emmy_Awards "33rd Daytime Emmy Awards") in April 2006, entertainer [Rosie O'Donnell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rosie_O'Donnell "Rosie O'Donnell") was introduced as a co-host for the show's tenth season;[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-30) she made her debut on September 5.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-31) After a string of controversies O'Donnell left the show in April 2007 due to failed renewal negotiations.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-rosie07-32) The following month, ABC stated that O'Donnell had asked to be let out of her contract three weeks before its expiration and that she had been granted permission to depart immediately.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-breakup-33)

### Seasons 11–18 (2007–2015)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_View&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Seasons 11–18 (2007–2015)")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/eb/Mullen_on_The_View.jpg/330px-Mullen_on_The_View.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Mullen_on_The_View.jpg)

The co-hosts interview U.S. Navy Adm. [Michael Mullen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Mullen "Michael Mullen") and his wife, Deborah, on November 24, 2010.

In August 2007, Walters replaced O'Donnell with actress [Whoopi Goldberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whoopi_Goldberg "Whoopi Goldberg") for season 11.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-WhoopiView-5) Goldberg debuted during the season premiere on September 4.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-34) Actress [Sherri Shepherd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sherri_Shepherd "Sherri Shepherd") joined as a permanent co-host beginning September 10.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-35) Hasselbeck went on [maternity leave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maternity_leave "Maternity leave") from October 2007 to January 2008 and again from August to October 2009, with rotating guest co-hosts filling in during the latter.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-37)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-38)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-39) In August 2009, Walters, Behar, Hasselbeck, Goldberg, and Shepherd won the [Daytime Emmy Award for Outstanding Talk Show Host](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daytime_Emmy_Award_for_Outstanding_Talk_Show_Host "Daytime Emmy Award for Outstanding Talk Show Host").[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-Hosts-40)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-Hosts2-41) Walters took a hiatus after undergoing open-heart surgery in May 2010 and returned on September 7 during the season 14 premiere broadcast.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-42)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-43)

In 2013, Behar left the series at the end of season 16.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-Deadline_Hollywood_Behar_Leaving-44) That same month, Hasselbeck was reported to be departing alongside Behar due to market research finding both of their views too "polarizing", which Walters denied.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-THR_Hasselbeck_departing-45)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-THRHasselbeck-46) Despite Walters' earlier denial, Hasselbeck indeed departed the show on July 10 to join the [Fox News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fox_News "Fox News") morning program _[Fox & Friends](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fox\_&\_Friends "Fox & Friends")_.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-47) Behar's final episode, a _[This Is Your Life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/This\_Is\_Your\_Life\_(American\_franchise) "This Is Your Life (American franchise)")_-style tribute to her, aired on August 9.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-48) Actress [Jenny McCarthy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jenny_McCarthy "Jenny McCarthy") became a co-host the following season and debuted on its premiere broadcast on September 9.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-49)

Walters retired on May 16, 2014.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-50)[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-goodbye-51) Shepherd and McCarthy departed the following month and made their final appearances on August 11.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-52)[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-53)

After making guest appearances during the previous season, actress [Rosie Perez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rosie_Perez "Rosie Perez") as well as former [White House Communications Director](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_House_Communications_Director "White House Communications Director")[Nicolle Wallace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicolle_Wallace "Nicolle Wallace") permanently joined the series in its 18th season,[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-54) establishing Perez as the series' first [Latina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hispanic_and_Latino_Americans "Hispanic and Latino Americans") co-host;[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-55) the two debuted alongside O'Donnell, who permanently returned, and Goldberg during the season premiere on September 15, 2014.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-56) Perez took a hiatus at the end of the year to rehearse for her role in the play _[Fish in the Dark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fish\_in\_the\_Dark "Fish in the Dark")_ and returned on February 3, 2015.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-57) That same month, representatives for O'Donnell confirmed that she would once again exit the panel due to "personal reasons"; her final appearance aired on February 12.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-58) Actress [Raven-Symoné](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raven-Symon%C3%A9 "Raven-Symoné") joined the series full-time in June after frequently guest co-hosting,[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-59) and the following month, comedian [Michelle Collins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelle_Collins_(comedian) "Michelle Collins (comedian)"), who had been a frequent guest, was permanently added for the following season.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-60) Perez and Wallace exited at the conclusion of the 18th season in August.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-61)[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-62)

### Seasons 19–30 (2015–present)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_View&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Seasons 19–30 (2015–present)")]

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/97/Whoopi_Goldberg_in_2024_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-Whoopi_Goldberg_in_2024_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Whoopi_Goldberg_in_2024_(cropped).jpg)

Entertainer [Whoopi Goldberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whoopi_Goldberg "Whoopi Goldberg") has co-hosted and moderated the series since 2007.

The 19th season saw the return of Behar as well as the addition of actress [Candace Cameron Bure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Candace_Cameron_Bure "Candace Cameron Bure") and broadcast journalist [Paula Faris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Faris "Paula Faris") as co-hosts alongside Goldberg, Raven-Symoné, and Collins,[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-nineteen-63) the lattermost of whom departed in June 2016.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-64) The following season began with eight rotating co-hosts: Behar, Goldberg, Raven-Symoné, Bure, Faris, television host [Sara Haines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sara_Haines "Sara Haines"), lawyer [Sunny Hostin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunny_Hostin "Sunny Hostin"), and television personality [Jedediah Bila](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jedediah_Bila "Jedediah Bila").[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-Variety-65)[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-Bure-66) Additionally, Behar began moderating on Fridays in Goldberg's place.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-67) On October 27, Raven-Symoné left the show to star in a [spin-off of the sitcom _That's So Raven_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raven's_Home "Raven's Home").[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-68) On December 8, Bure left the program, citing the commute between coasts and her commitments to other television projects as reasons;[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-Bure-66) her final episode as co-host aired the following day.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-farewell-69)

While Goldberg initially considered leaving after season 20,[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-Variety-65) she remained as moderator for season 21, with Behar, Faris, Haines, Hostin, and Bila all returning as co-hosts.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-TheView21-70)[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-71) On September 18, 2017, Bila exited the show on air.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-72) Television personality [Meghan McCain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meghan_McCain "Meghan McCain") subsequently joined the show after leaving her position at Fox News,[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-73) debuting as co-host on October 9.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-74) After giving birth to a daughter in December 2017, Haines returned from maternity leave in March 2018.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-75) Faris departed in July.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-76) In the same month, Haines left the show to co-host ABC's new third hour of its morning program _[Good Morning America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Good\_Morning\_America "Good Morning America")_;[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-77) she made her final appearance during the season's penultimate broadcast on August 2.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-78)

Broadcast journalist [Abby Huntsman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abby_Huntsman "Abby Huntsman") joined the panel in season 22, making her debut during the season premiere on September 4, 2018.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-79) Following an absence due to the death of [her father](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_McCain "John McCain"), McCain returned on October 8.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-80) Television personality [Ana Navarro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ana_Navarro "Ana Navarro") joined the show as a weekly guest co-host the following month.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-NavarroVariety-81)[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-best-82) Goldberg began a hiatus from co-hosting on February 7, 2019, due to pneumonia and sepsis, and returned on March 14.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-83)[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-84) Huntsman took maternity leave beginning in May.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-85)[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-86) Behar, Goldberg, Hostin, McCain, and Huntsman all returned for the 23rd season, which premiered on September 3.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-87) In January 2020, Huntsman departed to become a senior advisor to [her father's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jon_Huntsman_Jr. "Jon Huntsman Jr.")[2020 Utah gubernatorial election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Utah_gubernatorial_election "2020 Utah gubernatorial election") campaign;[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-88) she made her final appearance as co-host on January 17.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-89)

Haines returned as a guest co-host beginning in March 2020 and permanently rejoined the panel at the launch of the 24th season.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-90)[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-91)[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-studio-92) McCain gave birth to a daughter in September 2020 and returned in January 2021 after a three-month maternity leave.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-93)[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-94) After four years on the series, McCain departed at the end of the 24th season.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-95) She attributed her decision to her desire to raise her daughter in Washington D.C., to which she had relocated.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-96) McCain later cited the "toxic, direct and purposeful hostility" she experienced at the show as the reason for her exit.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-97) In April 2022, Goldberg took an extended hiatus from co-hosting to film the [Amazon Prime Video](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_Prime_Video "Amazon Prime Video") series _[Anansi Boys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anansi\_Boys\_(TV\_series) "Anansi Boys (TV series)")_.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-98) Starting in season 26, Navarro, who has been a weekly guest co-host since 2018, and political strategist [Alyssa Farah Griffin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alyssa_Farah_Griffin "Alyssa Farah Griffin") joined the show permanently. With the additions, the panel comprises six co-hosts.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-99)

## Production

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_View&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Production")]

During its first 17 seasons, _The View_ was filmed in ABC Television Studio 23 in New York City.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-100) The original set for the first four seasons was a leftover set from canceled soap opera _[The City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_City\_(1995\_TV\_series) "The City (1995 TV series)")_.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-101)[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-102) The panelists conduct discussions around a table or on a sofa and wear [IFB earpieces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interruptible_foldback "Interruptible foldback") through which producers communicate with them.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-WSJ-8)[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-103)[Bill Geddie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Geddie "Bill Geddie"), Barbara Walters' longtime producing partner, and Mark Gentile respectively served as showrunner and director for 17 years.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-VanityFair-3)[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-104)[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-105) Walters remained an executive producer until her death.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-106)

_The View_'s 18th season brought significant changes in a "creative overhaul" as well as a "new direction" for the show.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-revamp-107) In August 2014, ABC named [Bill Wolff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Wolff_(television_executive) "Bill Wolff (television executive)"), who had served as vice president of primetime programming at [MSNBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MSNBC "MSNBC") and as executive producer of the news and opinion program _[The Rachel Maddow Show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Rachel\_Maddow\_Show "The Rachel Maddow Show")_, the new executive producer, replacing Bill Geddie.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-108) Production of the show relocated to the ABC Broadcast Center on the [Upper West Side](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upper_West_Side "Upper West Side") of [Manhattan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhattan "Manhattan").[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-revamp-107)[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-109) During the season premiere on September 15, 2014, the series unveiled its new studio featuring a coffee table-style desk with low-arm chairs, a large video wall, in-the-round audience seating, and an on-camera social media station.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-110) Subsequent tweaks included a glass desk and high stools at center stage,[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-111) as well as color adjustments in backgrounds and graphics.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-112)[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-113)

In October 2014, ABC shifted production oversight on _The View_ from ABC's [daytime entertainment division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Daytime "ABC Daytime") to [Lincoln Square Productions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lincoln_Square_Productions "Lincoln Square Productions"), an [ABC News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_News_(United_States) "ABC News (United States)") subsidiary, where the show would be grouped under the division's non-fiction programming umbrella.[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-vty-114)[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-nyt-abcnewsview-115) The move allowed the show to leverage ABC News' resources toward news-related segments.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-116) In August 2015, former late-night talk show _[Late Show with David Letterman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Late\_Show\_with\_David\_Letterman "Late Show with David Letterman")_ producer [Brian Teta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_Teta "Brian Teta") joined the show as co-executive producer.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-117) Later in the month, executive producer Wolff departed the show.[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-118) In February 2016, along with the show's 20th season renewal, [Candi Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Candi_Carter "Candi Carter") was promoted to executive producer after serving as interim showrunner for season 19, becoming the first African-American executive producer in the show's history.[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-showrunner-119)

During the 20th-season premiere on September 6, 2016, the show debuted an updated set design with muted colors,[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-120)[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-121) retooled opening titles with footage of the co-hosts in a loft-like space,[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-122) as well as a new theme song entitled "World's Gone Crazy", written by [Diane Warren](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Warren "Diane Warren") and performed by [Mary J. Blige](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_J._Blige "Mary J. Blige").[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-123)[Hilary Estey McLoughlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilary_Estey_McLoughlin "Hilary Estey McLoughlin") was named senior executive producer in January 2017 after she was brought on as a consultant for season 19.[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-124) In September, Teta was promoted to executive producer ahead of the 21st-season premiere.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-TheView21-70) Sarah de la O serves as director, as of September 2019.[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-back-125) In March 2020, the series began airing without a live studio audience as a precaution in light of the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic").[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-126) Carter departed that same month to become the showrunner of the daytime talk show _[Tamron Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tamron\_Hall\_(talk\_show) "Tamron Hall (talk show)")_.[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-127) During the pandemic, the co-hosts broadcast from different locations, with Joy Behar, Whoopi Goldberg, Sunny Hostin, Meghan McCain, and Ana Navarro filming remotely, while Sara Haines remained in the studio, where Teta also still produced.[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-128)[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-129) McLoughlin exited in February 2021.[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-130)

For the series' 25th season, which began in September 2021, the co-hosts returned to filming in front of a live studio audience for the first time since March 2020.[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-131) The show also presented a new theme song entitled "For My Girls", written by Warren and performed by [Brandy Norwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brandy_Norwood "Brandy Norwood") and [Nicole Scherzinger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicole_Scherzinger "Nicole Scherzinger").[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-132)

For the series' 28th season, which premiered on September 3, 2024, _The View_ relocated from the ABC Broadcast Center to Studio B of Disney's new [7 Hudson Square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/7_Hudson_Square "7 Hudson Square") headquarters in Manhattan, serving as the first production to move to the new facility. The new studio extensively uses video walls along the walls and floors, allowing for more "dynamic" redressing of the entire set with different scenery using graphics. The existing desk was brought to the new studio, and was described as being the "jumping-off point" of the new studio's look and feel.[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-133)[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-134)[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-135) The show also debuted a new theme song entitled "This Version", written by Warren and performed by [Leona Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leona_Lewis "Leona Lewis").[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-136)

## Notable episodes

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_View&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Notable episodes")]

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d9/Barack_Obama_guests_on_The_View.jpg/330px-Barack_Obama_guests_on_The_View.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Barack_Obama_guests_on_The_View.jpg)

The co-hosts interview [Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama"), President of the United States, on July 29, 2010.

In 2010, U.S. President Barack Obama appeared as a guest on the show during the July 29 broadcast, marking the first appearance on a daytime talk show by a sitting U.S. president.[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-137) The episode also saw the return of Barbara Walters following her open heart surgery in May before she resumed her hiatus.[[138]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-138) On February 22, 2012, Star Jones came on as a guest and discussed her contentious exit from the show, marking her first appearance since said exit in 2006.[[139]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-CBS_News_Star_Jones_returns-139) On February 7, 2014, Rosie O'Donnell returned as a guest for the first time since quitting the show in 2007.[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-140) All eleven co-hosts in the show's history appeared during Walters' penultimate episode as co-host on May 15 to celebrate her retirement.[[141]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-141) Walters' final appearance as co-host aired the following day; it featured several guests, including Hillary Clinton and television host [Oprah Winfrey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oprah_Winfrey "Oprah Winfrey").[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-goodbye-51)

On March 27, 2015, the show celebrated its 4,000th broadcast, with Walters and Joy Behar returning for the celebration.[[142]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-View4000-142) On September 5, 2016, prior to the premiere of Season 20, ABC aired a documentary entitled _The View: 20 Years in the Making_, which featured notable moments from the show and several personalities involved in its history, hosted by Behar.[[143]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-143) On November 8, Behar, Jedediah Bila, Candace Cameron Bure, Sara Haines, and Sunny Hostin hosted a primetime [Election Night](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_elections "2016 United States elections") special of the show, which aired on [Lifetime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lifetime_(TV_network) "Lifetime (TV network)").[[144]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-144) On November 11, the series aired a "Flashback Friday" episode, which featured the original panel of co-hosts comprising Behar, Jones, Meredith Vieira, and Debbie Matenopoulos as well as a Veteran's Day tribute.[[145]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-secret-145)

In March 2017, the show had its first remote broadcast from [Walt Disney World](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walt_Disney_World "Walt Disney World") in [Orlando, Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orlando,_Florida "Orlando, Florida").[[146]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-146) Five episodes were filmed in front of the [Tree of Life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tree_of_Life_(Disney) "Tree of Life (Disney)") at [Disney's Animal Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disney's_Animal_Kingdom "Disney's Animal Kingdom"), featuring pre-recorded segments with Behar, Bila, Haines, Hostin, Paula Faris, and Whoopi Goldberg exploring [Epcot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epcot "Epcot"), [Magic Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magic_Kingdom "Magic Kingdom"), and [Disney's Hollywood Studios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disney's_Hollywood_Studios "Disney's Hollywood Studios").[[147]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-147) Film director [James Cameron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Cameron "James Cameron") came on as a guest on March 9, giving a preview of the themed area [Pandora – The World of _Avatar_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pandora_%E2%80%93_The_World_of_Avatar "Pandora – The World of Avatar").[[148]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-148) Other guests included Sherri Shepherd, Tom Bergeron, actresses [Ariel Winter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ariel_Winter "Ariel Winter"), [Audra McDonald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Audra_McDonald "Audra McDonald"), and [Mandy Moore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mandy_Moore "Mandy Moore"), actors [John Stamos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Stamos "John Stamos") and [Eric Stonestreet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Stonestreet "Eric Stonestreet"), and chefs [Masaharu Morimoto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masaharu_Morimoto "Masaharu Morimoto") and [Art Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Smith_(chef) "Art Smith (chef)"), with musical performances by singer [Andy Grammer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andy_Grammer "Andy Grammer") and rock band [Train](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Train_(band) "Train (band)").[[149]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-149)

On August 11, 2017, ABC re-aired the first episode of _The View_, which originally aired on the same date 20 years prior.[[150]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-150) On November 7, 2019, the series celebrated the airing of its 5,000th episode, with Bill Geddie, businessman [Donald Trump Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump_Jr. "Donald Trump Jr."), and television personality [Kimberly Guilfoyle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kimberly_Guilfoyle "Kimberly Guilfoyle") appearing as guests.[[151]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-151)[[152]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-152) The following month, singer [Darlene Love](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Darlene_Love "Darlene Love") performed her song "[Christmas (Baby Please Come Home)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christmas_(Baby_Please_Come_Home) "Christmas (Baby Please Come Home)")" alongside singer [Jason Derulo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jason_Derulo "Jason Derulo") on the December 20 broadcast, which Love has done annually since 2015.[[153]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-153)[[154]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-154) On March 11, 2020, the series aired its first broadcast without a live studio audience since its debut due to the COVID-19 pandemic.[[155]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-155)[[156]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-156)

On September 24, 2021, Hostin and Ana Navarro were removed from the show mid-broadcast due to testing positive for [COVID-19](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19 "COVID-19") before a planned in-person interview with U.S. Vice President [Kamala Harris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kamala_Harris "Kamala Harris"). The rest of the episode saw Behar and Haines answering audience questions and Harris appearing from a separate room in the studio building via a video stream during the last ten minutes.[[157]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-157) Hostin and Navarro returned the following week and said further testing indicated the two had received [false positive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/False_positive "False positive") results.[[158]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-158)

On June 2, 2022, the show aired a taped segment of Behar, Matenopoulos, Jones, and Vieira reuniting to reminisce at Essex Hall, where the original auditions for co-hosts took place.[[159]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-159) On January 3, 2023, the show aired a tribute special for Walters following her death on December 30, 2022. Former co-hosts Matenopoulos, Shepherd, and Ling appeared live on the show with former co-hosts Jones and Hasselbeck appearing virtually and Vieira calling into the show.[[160]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-160) The series aired its 6,000th episode in July 2024.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-six_thousand-1)

### Controversies

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_View&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Controversies")]

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e0/Rosie_O%27Donnell_2_by_David_Shankbone.jpg/250px-Rosie_O%27Donnell_2_by_David_Shankbone.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Rosie_O'Donnell_2_by_David_Shankbone.jpg)

[Rosie O'Donnell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rosie_O'Donnell "Rosie O'Donnell") was involved in multiple controversies during her time on _The View_.

The show's tenth season was embroiled in controversies,[[161]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-splitscreen-161) such as O'Donnell "speaking in [mock Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ching_chong#Modern_incidents "Ching chong")" as well as her public feud with businessman and later U.S. president [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump").[[162]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-162)[[163]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-rhetorical-163)[[164]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-feud-164) On May 17, 2007, O'Donnell sparked accusations of "[equating American soldiers with terrorists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_and_state_terrorism "United States and state terrorism")" in relation to the [Iraq War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iraq_War "Iraq War") by asking, "655,000 Iraqi civilians are dead. Who are the terrorists?"[[163]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-rhetorical-163)[[165]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-165) Following frequent debates involving O'Donnell and Elisabeth Hasselbeck, a confrontation ensued between the two on May 23 due to O'Donnell's issue with Hasselbeck's lack of willingness to defend her right to criticize the war.[[166]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-166) O'Donnell also stated that the media would portray her as "big, fat, lesbian, loud Rosie attacking innocent, pure, Christian Elisabeth" and that [Republican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_(United_States) "Republican Party (United States)") pundits were mischaracterizing her statements; Hasselbeck responded by telling O'Donnell to defend her own insinuations.[[161]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-splitscreen-161) O'Donnell exited the series two days later, three weeks earlier than scheduled.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-breakup-33) She later attributed her early exit to the use of a [split screen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Split_screen_(video_production) "Split screen (video production)") during the confrontation.[[167]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-167)

During a discussion about the [89th Miss America pageant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miss_America_2016 "Miss America 2016") on September 14, 2015, Michelle Collins called contestant [Kelley Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kelley_Johnson "Kelley Johnson")'s monologue about her occupation as a registered nurse "hilarious", stating that Johnson "read her emails out loud", while Behar referenced Johnson's attire and questioned why she had on "a doctor's stethoscope".[[168]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-168) The remarks resulted in an immediate social media backlash from the nursing profession, including the [hashtag](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hashtag "Hashtag") #NursesUnite.[[169]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-169)[[170]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-170) Two days later, Collins and Behar addressed the controversy on air.[[171]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-171) Consequently, pharmaceutical corporation [Johnson & Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnson_&_Johnson "Johnson & Johnson") and egg company [Eggland's Best](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eggland's_Best "Eggland's Best") pulled their sponsorships from the series,[[172]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-172) later followed by food company [McCormick & Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McCormick_&_Company "McCormick & Company"), laundry brand [Snuggle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snuggle "Snuggle"), and party store chain [Party City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Party_City "Party City").[[173]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-173)

On February 13, 2018, while analyzing television personality [Omarosa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Omarosa "Omarosa")'s comments in regards to U.S. Vice President [Mike Pence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Pence "Mike Pence")'s religiosity, Behar stated: "It's one thing to talk to Jesus, it's another thing when Jesus talks to you. That's called mental illness, if I'm not correct, hearing voices."[[174]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-intolerance-174) Content analysis organization [Media Research Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Media_Research_Center "Media Research Center") subsequently launched a campaign demanding an apology from Behar and urging viewers to do the same, resulting in 40,000 calls to ABC as well as 6,000 complaints to the show's advertisers.[[175]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-175) Pence himself responded and accused the show of expressing religious intolerance.[[174]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-intolerance-174)[The Walt Disney Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Walt_Disney_Company "The Walt Disney Company") CEO [Bob Iger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Iger "Bob Iger") later stated that Behar has directly apologized to Pence.[[176]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-176) On March 13, Behar issued an apology on air and said: "I think Vice President Pence is right; I was raised to respect everyone's religious faith, and I fell short of that. I sincerely apologize for what I said."[[177]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-177)

In February 2022, president of ABC News [Kim Godwin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kim_Godwin "Kim Godwin") suspended Goldberg from the show for two weeks after she stated during an episode that [the Holocaust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Holocaust "The Holocaust") was "not about race".[[178]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-178)[[179]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-179)

During a 2026 appearance on _The View_, [Pam Grier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pam_Grier "Pam Grier") claimed to have seen [lynched](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lynching_in_the_United_States "Lynching in the United States") bodies during her childhood in [Columbus, Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus,_Ohio "Columbus, Ohio"). These comments stirred controversy, as [America's Black Holocaust Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/America's_Black_Holocaust_Museum "America's Black Holocaust Museum") reports that the final recorded lynching in Ohio took place in 1911, decades before Grier's birth.[[180]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-180)

## Other media

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_View&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Other media")]

In 2016, [VH1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VH1 "VH1") picked up _[Daytime Divas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daytime\_Divas "Daytime Divas")_, a television series adaptation of Star Jones' book _Satan's Sisters_, which revolves around a fictional daytime talk show named _The Lunch Hour_ featuring five female co-hosts.[[181]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-vh1-181) Jones, who was also one of the series' executive producers, and then-_View_ co-hosts Joy Behar, Jedediah Bila, Sara Haines, and Sunny Hostin all made guest appearances on the series.[[182]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-182) It was canceled in 2017 after one season.[[183]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-183)

In September 2018, _The View_ began a [podcast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Podcast "Podcast") that saw the release of each episode in the show after its original televised broadcast.[[184]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-184) In September 2021, the series launched a companion podcast titled _Behind the Table_, which features conversations between former and current co-hosts.[[185]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-185) ABC began releasing episodes of _Behind the Table_ daily in September 2023.[[186]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-186)

In April 2019, [Thomas Dunne Books](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Dunne_Books "Thomas Dunne Books") published a non-fiction book entitled _[Ladies Who Punch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ladies\_Who\_Punch "Ladies Who Punch")_ by journalist Ramin Setoodeh, which chronicles the entire history of the show.[[187]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-187)[[188]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-188) It features interviews with various current and former _View_ co-hosts.[[189]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-189) The book is set to be adapted into a television miniseries.[[190]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-190)

## Criticism and reception

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_View&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Criticism and reception")]

### Critical response

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_View&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Critical response")]

A _[New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New\_York\_Times "New York Times")_ review, published ten days after the show premiered, describes what critic [Caryn James](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caryn_James "Caryn James") thought was distinctive about the show:

> The idea of women talking to one another on daytime television is not exactly radical. The idea that those women should be smart and accomplished is still odd enough to make _The View_ seem wildly different. It actively defies the bubbleheads-'R'-us approach to women's talk shows.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-nytimes-18)

In a 2001 profile of Barbara Walters for _[Vanity Fair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanity\_Fair\_(magazine) "Vanity Fair (magazine)")_, [James Wolcott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Wolcott "James Wolcott") called _The View_ a "genius bit of television".[[191]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-191) The following year, [Virginia Heffernan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia_Heffernan "Virginia Heffernan") of _[Slate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slate\_(magazine) "Slate (magazine)")_ complimented the chemistry between Walters, Meredith Vieira, Star Jones, and Joy Behar, writing that the women "have eased completely into the stock sensibility of middle-aged talk shows, embracing the imperatives that one be healthy, careful, temperate, charitable, and moderately cutesy while at the same time skeptical, ribald, and world-weary".[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-Slate-22)[Ken Tucker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ken_Tucker "Ken Tucker") of _[Entertainment Weekly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entertainment\_Weekly "Entertainment Weekly")_ praised the show in 2007, writing that it "does for daytime what _[The Daily Show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Daily\_Show "The Daily Show")_ does for nighttime: It reflects the pent-up frustrations, pleasures, and hostilities its audience has toward pop and political culture."[[192]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-192)

Despite being credited for helping the show achieve higher ratings, Rosie O'Donnell received criticism from "viewers and interest groups" that disagreed with her viewpoints.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-breakup-33)_[The Atlantic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Atlantic "The Atlantic")_'s Kevin O'Keefe deemed O'Donnell's hiring as moderator "somewhat curious" due to her being "such an outspoken individual".[[164]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-feud-164) Conversely, [Helena Andrews](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helena_Andrews "Helena Andrews") of _[Politico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politico "Politico")_ praised O'Donnell for making the show "actually watchable—something no longer relegated to the ether of [TiVo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TiVo "TiVo") or sneaked through head phones at work when we should be watching [CNN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CNN "CNN")".[[193]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-193) In 2014, Michael Schulman of _[The New Yorker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_Yorker "The New Yorker")_ highlighted O'Donnell's first tenure, elaborating that she "pushed the limits of what cheery daytime chatter could sustain, and _The View_ became more heated and more interesting as a result".[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-auto-7)

Jenny McCarthy's appointment as a co-host attracted backlash due to her anti-vaccination views.[[194]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-194)[[195]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-195) Writing as a senior science editor for _[HuffPost](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HuffPost "HuffPost")_, [David Freeman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Freeman_(journalist) "David Freeman (journalist)") referenced science communicator [Bill Nye](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Nye "Bill Nye")'s concern that McCarthy would "encourage parents to prevent their kids from getting vaccinated" as well has his hope that her views would be "discredited".[[196]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-Freeman-196)[Alex Pareene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Pareene "Alex Pareene") of _[Salon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salon\_(magazine) "Salon (magazine)")_ criticized the decision, writing that McCarthy "isn't just quirky—she spreads lies that hurt people".[[197]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-Pareene-197)[Jill Filipovic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jill_Filipovic "Jill Filipovic") remarked on _[The Guardian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Guardian "The Guardian")_ that McCarthy "has no record of political activism or even serious engagement with the world" other than her anti-vaccination stance.[[198]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-198)_The New Yorker_'s [Michael Specter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Specter "Michael Specter") asserted that ABC executives "should be ashamed of themselves for offering McCarthy a regular platform on which she can peddle denialism and fear to the parents of young children who may have legitimate questions about vaccine safety" and that her hiring was a "strike against reason and progress and hope".[[199]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-199)

Following Walters' retirement, the show became known for constant changes in its lineup of co-hosts,[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-nineteen-63)[[200]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-200) including the brief tenures of O'Donnell, McCarthy, Rosie Perez, Nicolle Wallace, and Michelle Collins.[[201]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-search-201) In July 2015, Daniel D'Addario of _[Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time\_(magazine) "Time (magazine)")_ suggested that it was time for ABC to end _The View_, citing the show's inability to sustain a consistent panel as a factor.[[202]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-202) The following year, _[Deadline Hollywood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deadline\_Hollywood "Deadline Hollywood")_'s [Lisa de Moraes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisa_de_Moraes "Lisa de Moraes") wrote that the series was "gaining a reputation as one of the riskier gigs for on-air talent".[[201]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-search-201)

In 2017, David Bauder of the [Associated Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Associated_Press "Associated Press") attributed the series' resurgence in viewership to its political discussions.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-comeback-6)_HuffPost_'s David Hinckley opined that _The View_ has been successful in implementing its original premise and maintaining "a balance in areas like ethnicity and ideology" in regards to its co-hosts.[[203]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-203) Writing for _The New York Times_ in May 2019, Amanda FitzSimons cited the fascination with the co-hosts as what sets the show apart from other entertainment and news programs and noted that it "remains one of the few places on TV where audiences can watch authentic human drama".[[204]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-204)[Lorraine Ali](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lorraine_Ali "Lorraine Ali") of the _[Los Angeles Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los\_Angeles\_Times "Los Angeles Times")_ praised the series for being "one of the few places left on TV where liberal, conservative and moderate voices pose questions that real folks might ask" and generating "raw moments that are as authentic as they are viral".[[205]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-205) In July 2021, _[Variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variety\_(magazine) "Variety (magazine)")_ columnist Daniel D'Addario found that the show had lost its "crackling electricity" and that the co-hosts had "veered into a place that wasn't even good TV" due to the limitations of taping remotely in response to the COVID-19 pandemic.[[206]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-206)

In July 2025, the conservative [Media Research Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Media_Research_Center "Media Research Center") released a study showing that 102 liberal-leaning guests and no conservative-leaning guests had been invited to the show during the first six months of 2025, a sharp departure from previous seasons.[[207]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-207)

### U.S. television ratings

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_View&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: U.S. television ratings")]

The tenth season of _The View_ averaged 3.5 million viewers per episode, with the season premiere being the series' most watched at 4.4 million viewers.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-rosie07-32)[[208]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-208) In November 2008, the show's post-election day telecast garnered the biggest audience in its history at 6.2 million in viewers, becoming the week's most-watched program in daytime television.[[209]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-209) It was surpassed by the broadcast on July 29, 2010, which featured President Barack Obama's first appearance as a guest and garnered 6.6 million viewers.[[210]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-Obama-210) In 2013, the show averaged 3.1 million daily viewers, which outpaced rival talk show _[The Talk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Talk\_(talk\_show) "The Talk (talk show)")_.[[211]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-211)[[212]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-30emmy-212) It averaged 4.1 million viewers during Walters' final week in May 2014, with the episode featuring a farewell to Walters on May 16 garnering 5.2 million viewers and ranking as the show's fourth most-watched broadcast.[[213]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-213)

The season 18 premiere in September 2014 drew the show's second largest season premiere audience to date of 3.902 million viewers.[[214]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-214)[[215]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-215) The ratings declined following the premiere, with those in the demographic of women 25–54 "pacing downward for the fourth straight season" and being 30 percent lower from five years prior.[[216]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-216) The ratings in the same demographic in January 2015 were down nine percent from the year prior.[[217]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-217) Season 19 averaged 2.757 million viewers per episode.[[218]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-reversed-218) The show averaged 2.94 million viewers during the first week of November 2016.[[145]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-secret-145) Its viewership during season 20 had been up five percent from the previous season by April 2017.[[218]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-reversed-218)

The 21st season attained the show's highest ratings since Walters' retirement, averaging 2.9 million viewers per episode.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-best-82) Its 5,000th episode, which aired in November 2019, garnered 3.021 million viewers.[[219]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-219) The series was one of the top five daytime talk shows in the U.S., with an average of 2.5 million daily viewers, as of January 2020.[[220]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-220) During the November 2020 [sweeps period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sweeps_period "Sweeps period"), it averaged 3.048 million viewers.[[221]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-221)_The View_ was the daytime talk or news program to obtain the highest number of total viewers during its 24th season, averaging 2.743 million viewers.[[222]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-222) As part of the 2022–2023 television season, the 26th season averaged 2.375 million viewers and ranked No. 1 in total viewers among all daytime talk programs. It was the series' third consecutive year in the position.[[223]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-223) At November 2025, the series was still getting c. 2.46 million viewers.[[224]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_View#cite_note-224)

Pre-Retirees: Plan Now for Health Care Costs

If you’re close to retirement, you’ll have several financial issues to consider. But you’ll want to pay attention to one of the
most important of these issues: health care costs. How can you prepare yourself for these expenses? First, get an early start
on estimating health care costs. More than two-thirds of those planning to retire in the next 10 years say they have no idea
what their health and long-term care costs will be in retirement, according to the Edward Jones/Age Wave Four Pillars of the
New Retirement study. And some people don’ t worry much about these costs, which may be considerable, thinking that
Medicare will pay for most of them.
While Medicare does cover many medical expenses, it also has its own costs. You probably won’ t pay a premium for Part A
(inpatient/hospital coverage), since you likely had this cost deducted from your paycheck when you were working. But if you
are hospitalized, you’ll have to pay deductibles and coinsurance (the percentage of costs you pay after you’ve paid your de-
ductible). Part B (doctor’s visits) requires a premium, deducted from your Social Security checks, and you must pay an out-
of-pocket deductible. After you meet this deductible for the year, you typically pay 20% of the Medicare-approved amount for
most doctor’s services. And when you enroll in Part D (prescription drug plan), you will likely also have to pay a monthly
premium, an annual deductible and coinsurance or copays.
To help pay for the Medicare deductible, coinsurance and copayments, you may want to get supplemental insurance,
known as Medigap. Premiums for Medigap vary, depending on the plan you choose.
As an alternative to original Medicare, you could select Medicare Advantage (sometimes called Part C). Medicare Advan-
tage plans are offered by private companies approved by
Medicare, but the benefits and costs vary by plan. These plans
generally will incorporate Medicare Parts A and B and will pro-
vide additional medical coverage, such as prescription drugs.
When you incorporate all the above, the annual out-of-pock-
et costs for traditional medical expenses likely will be about
$4,500 to $6,500 per year, per person – not insignificant, but
certainly a number that can be addressed by careful planning.
But there’s one more expense to keep in mind: long-term
care. The average cost of a private room in a nursing home is
more than $100,000 per year, according to the insurance
company Genworth. And Medicare typically pays few of these
expenses.
Clearly, between regular medical costs associated with
Medicare or those not covered by it, and costs resulting from
the possible need for long-term care, your health care bills can  IRA? Don't wait

Inspiration

The Heart of Winter

By Priscilla Hull

Suddenly, just like that, we are ensconced in winter.  November, and sometimes October, give us a taste
of what is to come.  We get some snow, sometimes, in this cold northland, we get a lot of snow, but gen-
erally the roads clear and things return to normal quickly.  This is just a taste of what's to come.  By
Thanksgiving it's cold, but not too cold. We enjoy the day and look forward with anticipation to the Decem-
ber holiday season, whatever we celebrate.  Stores are decorated with bows and bells and all kinds of
fancy trimmings.  We hardly notice that the days are getting shorter until December 21, the shortest day of
the year.  Even then, it hardly matters. It's only four days to the Big Day.  Spirits are high and kids are ex-
cited.  Yes, it's dark early, but there's so much to do; baking, wrapping, decorating!  They take most of our
attention.

Then, the Big Day is over.  Trees which only days before were the focus of our attention, are discarded
on the side of the road to be taken away by the trash men, maybe eaten by goats and pigs!  The lights are
taken down, or not lit anymore. Toys, new wished-for clothes are put away, some forgotten, and the world
returns to the grayness of winter.

Now, not even three weeks later, the world no longer shines with the lights of Christmas. It is cold, the kind of cold that soaks its way into our
bones.  The sky is eternal grey and winter storms bring more and more snow until driveways are narrow, walkways are treacherous and we are
searching for the sun!  This is the heart of winter!

It sounds sad and depressing doesn't it?  I offer an alternative.  The sun is visible a little longer. Even if it is hidden behind heavy cloud cover,
even if it doesn't send any warmth to the frozen landscape, it is there.  It is always waiting to send a ray of warmth to us.

Even in the heart (some say the dead) of winter, there are good things to be found.  It's time to read that book we got for Christmas; to learn how
to knit; to build something with the new tool; to make good with that New Year's resolution!  There's something new in this season.  Especially in this
time of restricted movements due to the virus restrictions, in this time of national and personal unrest, we should seek deeply within ourselves to
ﬁnd positive things to do. Ways to grow.  Things to learn.

Better days are coming.  It's up to us to make it happen.  It's our job to ﬁnd the new and the good in this new year, this new world of ours.  The
sun will be back. The snow will disappear.  Winter will fade away and be just a memory as we look ahead to ﬂowers, leaves, green grass and hon-
eybees!

He has made everything beautiful in its time.
Ecclesiastes 3:11

Priscilla Hull is the Lay Leader of the First United Methodist Church in Claremont, NH.

Pre-Retirees: Plan Now for Health Care Costs

If you’re close to retirement, you’ll have several financial issues to consider. But you’ll want to pay attention to one of the
most important of these issues: health care costs. How can you prepare yourself for these expenses? First, get an early start
on estimating health care costs. More than two-thirds of those planning to retire in the next 10 years say they have no idea
what their health and long-term care costs will be in retirement, according to the Edward Jones/Age Wave Four Pillars of the
New Retirement study. And some people don’ t worry much about these costs, which may be considerable, thinking that
Medicare will pay for most of them.
While Medicare does cover many medical expenses, it also has its own costs. You probably won’ t pay a premium for Part A
(inpatient/hospital coverage), since you likely had this cost deducted from your paycheck when you were working. But if you
are hospitalized, you’ll have to pay deductibles and coinsurance (the percentage of costs you pay after you’ve paid your de-
ductible). Part B (doctor’s visits) requires a premium, deducted from your Social Security checks, and you must pay an out-
of-pocket deductible. After you meet this deductible for the year, you typically pay 20% of the Medicare-approved amount for
most doctor’s services. And when you enroll in Part D (prescription drug plan), you will likely also have to pay a monthly
premium, an annual deductible and coinsurance or copays.
To help pay for the Medicare deductible, coinsurance and copayments, you may want to get supplemental insurance,
known as Medigap. Premiums for Medigap vary, depending on the plan you choose.
As an alternative to original Medicare, you could select Medicare Advantage (sometimes called Part C). Medicare Advan-
tage plans are offered by private companies approved by
Medicare, but the benefits and costs vary by plan. These plans
generally will incorporate Medicare Parts A and B and will pro-
vide additional medical coverage, such as prescription drugs.
When you incorporate all the above, the annual out-of-pock-
et costs for traditional medical expenses likely will be about
$4,500 to $6,500 per year, per person – not insignificant, but
certainly a number that can be addressed by careful planning.
But there’s one more expense to keep in mind: long-term
care. The average cost of a private room in a nursing home is
more than $100,000 per year, according to the insurance
company Genworth. And Medicare typically pays few of these
expenses.
Clearly, between regular medical costs associated with
Medicare or those not covered by it, and costs resulting from
the possible need for long-term care, your health care bills can  IRA? Don't wait

Inspiration

The Heart of Winter

By Priscilla Hull

Suddenly, just like that, we are ensconced in winter.  November, and sometimes October, give us a taste
of what is to come.  We get some snow, sometimes, in this cold northland, we get a lot of snow, but gen-
erally the roads clear and things return to normal quickly.  This is just a taste of what's to come.  By
Thanksgiving it's cold, but not too cold. We enjoy the day and look forward with anticipation to the Decem-
ber holiday season, whatever we celebrate.  Stores are decorated with bows and bells and all kinds of
fancy trimmings.  We hardly notice that the days are getting shorter until December 21, the shortest day of
the year.  Even then, it hardly matters. It's only four days to the Big Day.  Spirits are high and kids are ex-
cited.  Yes, it's dark early, but there's so much to do; baking, wrapping, decorating!  They take most of our
attention.

Then, the Big Day is over.  Trees which only days before were the focus of our attention, are discarded
on the side of the road to be taken away by the trash men, maybe eaten by goats and pigs!  The lights are
taken down, or not lit anymore. Toys, new wished-for clothes are put away, some forgotten, and the world
returns to the grayness of winter.

Now, not even three weeks later, the world no longer shines with the lights of Christmas. It is cold, the kind of cold that soaks its way into our
bones.  The sky is eternal grey and winter storms bring more and more snow until driveways are narrow, walkways are treacherous and we are
searching for the sun!  This is the heart of winter!

It sounds sad and depressing doesn't it?  I offer an alternative.  The sun is visible a little longer. Even if it is hidden behind heavy cloud cover,
even if it doesn't send any warmth to the frozen landscape, it is there.  It is always waiting to send a ray of warmth to us.

Even in the heart (some say the dead) of winter, there are good things to be found.  It's time to read that book we got for Christmas; to learn how
to knit; to build something with the new tool; to make good with that New Year's resolution!  There's something new in this season.  Especially in this
time of restricted movements due to the virus restrictions, in this time of national and personal unrest, we should seek deeply within ourselves to
ﬁnd positive things to do. Ways to grow.  Things to learn.

Better days are coming.  It's up to us to make it happen.  It's our job to ﬁnd the new and the good in this new year, this new world of ours.  The
sun will be back. The snow will disappear.  Winter will fade away and be just a memory as we look ahead to ﬂowers, leaves, green grass and hon-
eybees!

He has made everything beautiful in its time.
Ecclesiastes 3:11

Priscilla Hull is the Lay Leader of the First United Methodist Church in Claremont, NH.
